          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. These matters pertain to varied service conditions of serving
and retired judicial officers of different States and the issues to
be dealt with by this Court arise on a pan-India basis.
2. Since various issues raised are overlapping in the two pending
batches of cases, it is directed that W.P.(C) No.1022/1989 and W.P.
(C) No.643/2015, as well as the matters connected thereto, which
relate to method of recruitment, service conditions, pension and
pay scale of district judiciary, and other aspects of judicial
service, be tagged and heard together. W.P.(C) No.1022/1989 shall
be treated as the main case.
3. We  have  requested  Mr.  Siddharth  Bhatnagar  and  Mr.  K.
Parameshwar, learned  Amicus  Curiae  in the respective cases to
prepare a common brief note on the pending applications/issues in
these two matters. Through the said note, they shall categorise the
pending applications as well as connected writ petitions/special
leave petitions/cases as per the issue(s) involved therein. Such
effort would, then, enable this Court to proceed issue-wise and
bring closure to the pending disputes.
4. For this purpose, we direct the Registry to ensure that
28

## Page 98

digital copies of all the I.A.s and connected petitions are
supplied to the learned amici so that they may prepare the note
expeditiously.
5. Having observed so, we hasten to add that the issue re:
enhancement of the age of superannuation for officers in the
District Judiciary is already scheduled to be finally heard on
01.09.2026. Thereafter, the matters pertaining to the service
conditions of the ‘E-Courts Technical Staff’ are scheduled to be
heard on 02.09.2026. In the course of hearing, the lack of
uniformity in the applicable pension scheme has been highlighted,
which has been captured in SLP(C) No. 20781/2018 and SLP(C) Nos.
6471-6473/2020. These SLPs are hereby directed to be listed on
03.11.2026.
6. We would appreciate it if the learned amici curiae  file their
common note on the categorization of the issues by 11.09.2026,
whereupon W.P.(C) No. 1022/1989 and W.P.(C) No. 643/2015 shall be
listed on 16.09.2026 for further directions.
7. This Court, at this juncture, is constrained to note that
various judicial officers, whether in individual capacity or as a
group, are approaching this Court at the first instance for
redressal of their grievances. It appears to us that this has taken
place,  in  the  majority  of  cases,  due  to  a  lack  of  timely
initiatives or redressive action by the Administrative Committees
(or any other analogous Committee) of the respective High Court(s).
We, therefore, request the Chief Justices of all the High Courts to
sensitise their Administrative/other Committees to deal with the
pending  issues  regarding  service  conditions  of  the  judicial
29

## Page 99

officers and take an appropriate decision.  
8. It goes without saying that in case the High Court resolves
that the judicial officers, serving or retired, are entitled to any
particular pay or other benefits, such recommendation shall be
forthwith made to the State Government. It is only if there is an
inaction on the part of the State Government(s) in giving effect to
such recommendations that judicial interference may be warranted.
For that purpose, the affected/aggrieved judicial officers may
approach the jurisdictional High Courts.
9. Meanwhile,  with  a  view  to  permit  the  learned  amici to
effectively  identify  the  pending  issues  and  complete  their
categorization, the Registry shall not entertain any I.A./M.A. in
these matters. In case a judicial officer/representative body seeks
to make a prayer regarding an issue which this Court is already
seized of through an existing application, they shall also be
permitted to place their submissions regarding the same.
10. It goes without saying that if due to any prior order in the
instant petitions, the judicial officer/organization is required to
raise the respective grievances before this Court, the same may be
done through an independent petition. Such a petition shall,
however, not be entertained by the Registry of this Court unless an
advance copy thereof is also supplied to the learned amici curiae.
(NITIN TALREJA)                           (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        DY. REGISTRAR

BHOPAL MUNICIPAL CORPORATION APPELLANT(S)
        VERSUS
DR SUBHASH C. PANDEY & ORS. RESPONDENT(S)
WITH
CIVIL APPEAL NO.   7728 OF 2023  
1. Read  the  Orders  dated  11.02.2026,  19.02.2026,
29.04.2026, 05.05.2026 and 25.05.2026 in the present
case. 
2. In compliance with the above Orders, the Supreme
Court Monitoring Committee (SCMC), through the Member
Secretary, CPCB, has placed on record the Affidavit
dated  05.08.2026  and  the  Interim  Report  for  the
period  ending  03.08.2026.  We  have  perused  the
Affidavit and the Reports and note that the Supreme
Court Monitoring Committee, giving full effect to the
Orders  of this  Court read  with the  Solid Waste
Management Rules, 2026, has communicated, initiated,
and put in place the Statutory Committees for the
implementation and enforcement of the SWM Rules,
2026.  These  initiatives  are  steps  in  the  right
direction. However, the larger and perennial hazards

## Page 140

2
Civil Appeal No.  6174/2023
arising from the non-observance of the SWM Rules,
2026, by the stakeholders are not addressed by merely
putting in place Committees and Enforcement Agencies.
The SCMC has scaled the mountains and also fathomed
the problem. The mounds of garbage is the problem
demanding the attention of everyone. Therefore, the
question we ask today, not just to those impleaded as
Respondents  to  the  present  proceedings,  but  to
everyone within the jurisdiction of this Court, is,
“whose task is it?” for the successful implementation
of the SWM Rules, 2026.
3. In our previous substantive Order, we noted that “ The
singularity of obligation and compliance under the
SWM Rules, 2026, is that every human being and their
activities result in pollution, yet all contributors
expect a minuscule percentage of sanitary workers to
handle it. This perception shall be eradicated, and
it shall be the responsibility of all contributors to
Solid Waste to manage and be part of the Rules”. This
is  clearly  lacking  among  individuals  and
institutions,  including  schools  and  colleges,
students,  the  educated  and  the  illiterate,  the
employed  and  the  unemployed,  and  finally,
professionals and businessmen. It is regrettable that

## Page 141

3
Civil Appeal No.  6174/2023
across society, the general feeling is “I am entitled
to generate but not to cooperate and control the
impact of solid waste management at the threshold”.
4. To wit, India’s population exceeds 1.4 billion, with
varying  levels  of  literacy,  education  and  civic
infrastructure.  Every  person,  household  and
institution (without exception) generates solid waste
as an inevitable by-product of life and activity. The
volume  and  complexity  of  such  waste,  i.e.,
biodegradable,  non-biodegradable,  hazardous,
electronic and construction, have outgrown what any
single class of workers can be expected to absorb or
handle. The infrastructure needs a complete audit and
upgradation to meet the extant standards of the SWM
Rules, 2026.
5. The  prevailing  assumption  that  Solid  Waste  is  a
problem for sanitary workers alone, while the rest of
the population remains passive generators, is neither
legally correct nor practically sustainable, and is
constitutionally  unethical.  Continued  complacency
will lead to pandemic and endemic situations. With
this in mind, Rule 4 of the SWM Rules, 2026 casts the
duty of segregation, safe storage and hand-over on

## Page 142

4
Civil Appeal No.  6174/2023
every  waste  generator,  a  term  covering  every
individual, household, institution and establishment.
This statutory duty is reinforced by Article 51A(g)
of the Constitution of India and is inseparable from
the right to a clean and healthy environment under
Article 21 of the Constitution of India. The Court is
enforcing  SWM  Rules,  2026  through  continuous
Mandamus,  prevent  pollution  from  solid  waste  to
environment including Rivers. The SCMC is directed to
focus  on  water  pollution  from  Municipal  Solid
Wastes/Materials to Rivers and place before the Court
data for further directions.
6. Law can secure cooperation only by prescribing rules
and consequences. It cannot, by itself, generate
civic behaviour. Compliance is achieved only when the
individual and institutional generators internalize
the obligation. To this end, the SCMC has addressed
letters to all the Chief Secretaries/Secretaries of
the States and Union Territories. Notably, the SCMC
has also addressed letters to all the Ministries,
viz., Indian Railways/Public Sector Undertakings. We
categorise these as State, Instrumentalities of the
State and Government/Public Companies. Insofar as
these Departments are concerned, we call upon the

## Page 143

5
Civil Appeal No.  6174/2023
SCMC to stipulate an outer limit of six weeks from
even date for reporting the status of compliance with
the directives issued by the SCMC. The real problem
lies  in  the  unorganised  sector  of  residential,
commercial and business establishments. Through the
Order of even date, we reiterate that this Court, in
its constitutional obligation and power, has directed
the delegation of powers to the District Collectors
under Section 5 of the Environment Protection Act,
1986. The Disaster Management Act, 2005 is referred
to in our earlier orders. The Parliament, in its
wisdom,  after  realising  the  difficulties  in
controlling industrial pollution, has incorporated
Section 5 in the EP Act. The practical reasoning and
objective are that unabated and uncontrolled air and
water pollution can be controlled and abated through
the  stoppage  of  industrial  activity.  The
administrative  machinery  constituted  below  is  a
scaffold  to  accelerate  that  internalisation.
Indefinite, exclusive reliance on State supervision
of a constitutionally literate citizenry would defeat
the object of the Rules.
a. Step 1: Powers under Section 5 of the EP Act to
District  Collectors,  and  under  Section  23  for

## Page 144

6
Civil Appeal No.  6174/2023
supervision through Special Cells, etc., already
implemented.
b. Step 2: Realisation of the object through universal
compliance  by  every  individual.  Order  to  be
understood as active, not passive. 
c. Step 3: For this purpose, SCMC through the Chief
Secretary(ies)  of  the  State(s),  directs  the
District Collectors to identify all bulk waste
generators/  BWGs  within  their  respective
jurisdictions,  in  cooperation  with  the  Local
Bodies, within six weeks from today.
d. Step 4: The SCMC, through the Chief Secretary(ies)
of the State(s) directs the District Collector(s)
to communicate to all the bulk waste generators/
BWGs the consequences of non-compliance with SWM
Rules,  2026  which  consequence  would  include
temporary disconnection of power or water supply
until  the  waste  generated  by  the  bulk  waste
generators conforms to the SWM Rules.
 
e. Step 5: The objective of communication, as stated
in Step 4, is to enable the BWGs to set up required

## Page 145

7
Civil Appeal No.  6174/2023
facilities in place and to report online compliance
to the local bodies for inspection and forwarding
the report to the District Collector(s).
f. Step 6: The SCMC directs the District Collectors to
enhance  the  participation  of  the  elected
representatives of the wards of Gram Panchayats,
Municipalities  and  the  Corporations  in  the
implementation of the Rules. The ULBs/MLBs/RLBs are
directed to notify the waste generated, accounted
for and unaccounted for, and the steps taken to
achieve  100%  basic  participation  by  the
stakeholders referred to in paragraph 3 (supra).
7. Every  local  body  shall,  through  its
Chairman/Commissioner/Secretary, as directed by the
jurisdictional  District  Collector,  communicate  in
writing  to  every  BWG  within  its  limits  the
obligations  viz,  (i)  segregation,  storage  and
handover  of  solid  waste  generated;  and  (ii)  the
consequence  of  non-compliance  resulting  in  the
temporary  disconnection  of  water  and  electricity
supply by order of the District Collector’s Special
Cell, restorable upon submission of a compliance
certificate by the BWG.

## Page 146

8
Civil Appeal No.  6174/2023
8. The  District  Collectors  need  more  sentinels  and
teachers to achieve a change in approach and attitude
among our citizenry towards solid waste management.
Therefore, the compulsion is to educate,  educate,
educate school and college students to enrol their
family members for the implementation of the SWM
Rules, 2026. The Interim Report filed refers to the
correspondence on this subject. But the need is to
transform the correspondence into action. The slow
approach of the Education Department is slightly
unintelligible  and  troubling  the  Court.  The
Department of School and Higher Education shall, with
immediate  effect,  integrate  both  theoretical  and
practical knowledge on Solid Waste Management for
students to train their family members, and also
train teachers as trainers. The trained students
would function as household-level supervisors. This
Court  notes that  an educated  child is  the most
effective and least coercive instrument for educating
a parent or a relative for the implementation of
Solid Waste Management. It is for their future and
health  that  the  student  is  entrusted  with  this
responsibility. Periodical audits are conducted by
the District Education Departments, and reports are

## Page 147

9
Civil Appeal No.  6174/2023
submitted to the jurisdictional District Collectors.
9. IT/Digitally enabled non-passive reporting.  Note: A
portal is already in place. The Authorities consider
including geotagged photographs of waste accumulation
and monthly compliance reports through the chain,
i.e., District Collector → State Secretary and Union
Ministries.
10. The Order is, without delay, translated into regional
languages and communicated to all, as directed in the
previous Orders of this Court.
11. Sectoral compliance from Railways, Defence, and other
Ministries is monitored by SCMC. 
12. The objective of the present order is to sunset and
transition to self-regulation.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.001202-001203 OF 2023
THE STATE OF NCT OF DELHI ……… APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
MADHU GUPTA & ANR. ……… RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. We have heard Mr. Abhishek Singh, learned counsel
for the appellant and Mr. Rajeev Kumar Bansal, learned
counsel appointed as legal aid counsel by the Supreme
Court  Legal  Services  Committee  to  represent  the
respondents.
2. State  is  in  appeal  being  aggrieved  by  the
judgment  of  reversal  by  the  High  Court  of  Delhi
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter). Be it stated
that respondent Nos. 1 and 2 were convicted under
Sections 302 and 201, read with Section 34 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’) by the Trial
Court vide the judgment and order dated 18.03.2017 and
sentenced to undergo life imprisonment vide the order
1

## Page 168

of sentence dated 21.03.2017. This came to be reversed
by the High Court on appeal by the respondents and they
have been acquitted of all the charges. 
3. The case of the prosecution is that in the late
evening of 12.09.2008  at about 11:00 pm, a first
information  was  received  at  the  concerned  police
station that from the room of the tenant, red and black
watery  substance  was  coming  out.  When  the  police
reached the room and opened the same, they found the
dead body of a male smeared in blood. The landlord
identified the dead body as that of his tenant Bijender
@ Virender.
4. It appears that on 11.09.2008, a scuffle had
taken place in the tenanted premises between Bijender
Gupta and Madhu on the one hand with the deceased
Satender @ Nanhey on the other hand. On that fateful
night, Satender @ Nanhey along with Bijender @ Virender
had taken dinner together. After dinner when all of
them had gone to sleep, it appears that Satender @
Nanhey  tried  to  take  advantage  of  his  physical
proximity with the daughter of Madhu. This led to
altercation between Satender @ Nanhey and Madhu which
later on escalated into a scuffle. At that stage,
2

## Page 169

Bijender @ Virender also joined Madhu in assaulting
Satender @ Nanhey which led to his death. It has also
come on record that Bijender @ Virender had dressed up
the dead body of Satender @ Nanhey with his clothes to
give the appearance that the dead body was his.
5. The Trial Court after considering the evidence on
record convicted the respondents as above. 
6. In appeal before the High Court, the evidence of
the son of Bijender @ Virender, Master Sumit (PW-5),
and the daughter of Madhu, (K), were re-appreciated.
Deposition of PW-5, Master Sumit, as analyzed by the
High Court is as under:
15.  Master  Sumit  (PW-5),  son  of
Virender, aged about 10 years, stated
that  he  used  to  live  in  a  tenanted
accommodation having two rooms along his
father Virender only while mother Neelam
used to live at her parental house. He
had a step mother but he didn't know her
name. His step mother also resided with
them. “K" was his sister.
He did not know where “K" used to reside
when  he  along  with  his  father  was
residing at Village Bajidpur. During his
cross  examination,  he  denied  that  he
3

## Page 170

stated  to  the  police  that  on  10 th
September, 2008, Madhu gave a telephone
call on the mobile phone to his father
and told him that she had taken into
confidence the deceased Stender @ Nanhe
and requested his father to reach there
and he will reach within 1-2 hours. He
also  denied  the  suggestion  that  when
they had gone to fetch cold drink, they
met his uncle Sanju on their way or that
his father told Sanju about the visit of
Nanhe and further instructed Sanju to
introduce Nanhe as the friend of his
brother that his uncle Sanju asked his
father not to kill Satender @ Nanhe and
to  leave  him  unhurt  or  that  after
purchasing cold drink and rice, he along
with his father and sister returned or
that  thereafter,  they  all  drank  cold
drink and tea or that they were served
dinner or that they were asked to sleep
in other room or that Virender asked his
uncle Sanju to sleep on the terrace or
that his sister “K", Madhu, his father
and Nanhe slept in one room or that he
went to the room of his neighbour.
7. Similarly, PW-7, the daughter of Madhu in her
evidence and cross-examination deposed in the following
manner:
16. “K” (PW-7), aged around 13 years,
4

## Page 171

stated that the name of her mother was
Madhu. She did not know anything about the
present case. She did not know Virender or
Satender @ Nanhe. She was not present at
the time of the incident. She was residing
with her nani Urmila for the last two and
a half years when her mother left her
there. During her cross-examination, she
denied the suggestion that when she and
her brother Sumit were of tender age, her
mother Madhu had taken her to village
Kisol  at  Ghaziabad  to  the  house  of
deceased Satender @ Nanhe at Ghaziabad.
7.1. She was further cross-examined which is as
under:
17. On  further  cross  examination “K”
stated that the deceased and her mother
lived together for about 10 years prior
to the incident. She was living with the
deceased in the absence of her mother
Madhu as well. When she was a minor, she
did not know if there was any quarrel
between  her  mother  and  the  deceased.
Later  on,  there  was  quarrel  between
them. By later on, she meant when Nanhe
tried to misbehave with her, then her
mother started quarreling with him, "Jab
Nanhe ne mere saath galat harkat karne
ki koshish ki tou meri ma ka uske saath
jhagra hone laga". After the incident of
5

## Page 172

misbehaviour, she along with her mother
started  living  separately.  When  she
along  with  her  mother  started  living
separately with Virender, Nanhe started
visiting there also. She admitted that
the  last  day  Nanhe  visited  the  said
place  i.e.  Bazid  Pur  was  when  the
present incident took place. On the date
of  incident,  she  with  her  mother,
Virender, Sumit and another person whose
name she did not know were present at
the tenanted room. On the night when she
along  with  her  mother,  Virender  and
Nanhe was sleeping in the room, "Nanhe
ne mere saath galat harkat ki aur chhed
chhad karne laga". Her mother also woke
up.  Her  mother  and  Nanhe  started
quarreling with each other. Nanhe caught
hold  of  her  mother  by  her  neck  and
pushed her. The head of her mother hit
the  wall.  Virender  also  woke  up.
Thereafter, Virender and Nanhe started
grappling with each other (haatha pai ho
gayi).  Grappling  continued  for  a
considerable time,  where after,  Nanhe
fell  down  on  the  floor  and  became
unconscious. After that, they all left
the room. Her parents dropped her at the
house of her aunt.
8. The High Court after an assessment of the evidence,
6

## Page 173

came to the conclusion that the 2 respondents had
exercised their right of private defence in a situation
where there was grave and sudden provocation. In the
process, the deceased suffered fatal injuries. The High
Court held thus:
22. A perusal of the prosecution evidence
itself  reveals  that  when  the  deceased
tried to sexually molest the daughter of
appellant Madhu a scuffle ensued wherein
Madhu received an injury, where after a
further  scuffle  ensued  between  the
deceased and Virender as a consequence
whereof due to the grappling and manual
strangulation of the neck, deceased fell
down. In view of the nature of injury
which was not pre-determined but on the
spur of the moment, it cannot be held
that there was common intention of the
appellants Madhu and Virender to commit
murder of the deceased.
Therefore, the impugned judgment convicting
the appellants for offence punishable under
Section 302/34 IPC cannot be sustained.
9. The High Court, therefore, over-turned the finding
of conviction rendered by the Trial Court under Sections
302/34 IPC and acquitted the respondents.
9.1. It may be mentioned that the High Court also
7

## Page 174

interfered with the conviction of the respondents under
Section 201 IPC and acquitted them of the same. The
High Court held thus:
34. The essential ingredient for an act
punishable  under  Section  201  IPC  is
commission of an offence. Since no offence
has been committed in the present case and
the appellants have been acquitted for
offences punishable under Section 302 IPC
or any other minor offence thereof for
causing death of Satender @ Nanhe, it
cannot be held that the appellants have
caused destruction of the evidence after
committing the offence.
10. Learned counsel for the State submits that the
response of the respondents was disproportionate which
led to the death of the deceased and, therefore,
respondents are not entitled to the benefit of the
exception of Section 96 of the IPC.
11. We are not impressed by the submission made by
learned counsel for the State. We have independently
analyzed the evidence on record and we find that the
view taken by the High Court is a plausible one. It
would  be  reasonable  to  take  the  view  that  the
respondents acted in self-defence leading to the death
of the deceased, which act is covered by Section 96 IPC
8

## Page 175

read with the third description of Section 100 thereof.
Evidently, when two views are possible, the view in
favour of the accused should be preferred.
12. That being the position, we find no merit in the
appeals.
13. Criminal appeals are accordingly dismissed.
14. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
National Consumer Commissions
1. It has come to our attention that a recent news item has
highlighted certain issues concerning the slow disposal rate of
cases and poor performance of the National Consumer Commissions.
Therefore, in view of the inordinate delay in disposal of pending
matters, especially when, in some cases, hearings are not taking
place for years, we request the Presidents of the National Consumer
Commissions to send a report providing necessary and relevant
details with respect to: (i) the total pendency of cases; (ii) the
composition of the Commissions; (iii) the average disposal rate of
8

## Page 185

the matters by different Benches; (iv) the estimated time likely to
be required for disposal of the pending matters; and, (v) whether
there is a need for increasing the strength of the Commissions.  
2. We would appreciate it if the aforesaid report were sent
within two weeks.
State Consumer Commissions
3. Learned  Amicus  Curiae  will  also  furnish,  separately,
information with respect to the pendency of cases before the State
Consumer Commissions and the vacancies therein.  The information
should also indicate the oldest pending matters.  The pendency
chart should also further provide the year-wise pendency.  The
Presidents of the State Consumer Commissions are requested to
furnish the requisite information to the learned  Amicus  Curiae.
The  Department  of  Consumer  Affairs  of  the  respective  State
Governments will also assist the learned Amicus Curiae in collating
the said information.  
4. Learned  Amicus  Curiae  may also contact Mr. Anupam Mishra,
Joint Secretary, Department of Consumer Affairs, who was earlier
appointed as the Nodal Officer to assist this Court.  He may also
provide the requisite information.
5. The Presidents of the State Consumer Commissions are requested
to forward the performance evaluation report for the last three
years of the District Consumer Forums under their respective
jurisdictions.
6. List on 02.09.2026 along with SMW(C) No.2/2021.  
7. Having regard to the multiplicity of issues involved and the
9

## Page 186

fact that SMW(C) No.2/2021 has also been ordered to be listed along
with this case, we appoint Ms. Prerna Priyadarshini and Ms. Shivani
Vij, learned AORs, to also assist this Court in these matters as
Amicus Curiae.
(NITIN TALREJA)                           (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)

O R D E R
1) Leave granted.
2) The appellants were convicted by the
Trial  Court  for  the  offences
punishable  under  Sections  148  and
302/149 of the Indian Penal Code, 1980
in S.T. No. 224 of 2008 on the file of
the  Additional  Sessions  Judge-VII,
1

## Page 188

Dhanbad.  They  were  accordingly
sentenced  to  undergo  rigorous
imprisonment for life and fine.  This
has been confirmed by the High Court
vide  the impugned order.  Aggrieved,
the appellants are before us.  
3) We  have  heard  the  learned  Senior
Counsel appearing for the appellants
and the learned counsel appearing for
the respondent.
4) The case of the prosecution is that
the  appellants  along  with  the  co-
accused attacked the deceased on the
head with swords and iron rods.
5) The learned Senior Counsel appearing
for the appellant submitted that it is
2

## Page 189

rather strange that an application has
been filed by the respondent to recall
the order passed by this Court dated
19.11.2025  in  SLP  (Crl)  No.
14822/2025, wherein the sentence of a
co-accused  has  been  suspended  on
merits. It is further submitted that a
decree has been passed in favour of
the appellant(s) and that the appeal
before the High Court is of the year
2025.  The appellants have undergone
more than two years of incarceration. 
6) Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
respondent-State submits that taking
note of the overt act attributed to
the appellants, there is no need for
interference with the impugned order.
3

## Page 190

7) Upon  hearing  the  learned  Senior
Counsel appearing for the appellants
and the learned counsel appearing for
the respondent, we are inclined to set
aside the impugned order, and suspend
the sentence of the appellants during
the pendency of the appeal before the
High Court, as the appeal is of the
year 2025 and will take considerable
length  of  time  to  be  disposed  of.
Further, the appellants have undergone
more than two years of incarceration.
We also take note of the overt act
attributed to the appellants and the
fact  that  this  is  a  case  where  a
decree has been passed in favour of
the appellant(s) as against the side
4

## Page 191

of the deceased.
8) In  such  view  of  the  matter,  the
impugned order stands set aside and
the  sentence  of  the  appellants  is
suspended and they are granted bail
during  the  pendency  of  the  appeal
before the High Court.  
9) Accordingly,  the  appeal  stands
allowed.
10) Pending application(s), if any, shall
stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S).       OF 2026

VIKAS MAHENDRASINGH SAINI                 …Appellant(s)

UMADEVI DURGAPRASD KESHRWANI & ORS.     …Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. This appeal is against the judgment and order passed by the
High Court of Judicature at Bombay, Nagpur Bench in Writ Petition
No. 6401 of 2022 dated 11.12.2025. The Writ Petition was filed
against the order dated 16.09.2021 passed by the Trial Court rejecting
the appellant’s/plaintiff’s application under Order VI Rule 17 of the
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (for short ‘CPC’) for amendment of
plaint. 
3. Facts that are relevant for disposal of the present appeal are as
follows: The Appellant instituted a suit for declaration, permanent
1

## Page 231

injunction and cancellation of a certain sale deed and also for a
decree of possession. The defendants contested the suit by filing a
written statement and after the issues were formulated on 23.01.2014,
the suit went for trial. During the course of trial, the appellant filed his
affidavit of evidence and sought to introduce certain other documents.
Apart from others, the plaintiff sought to exhibit a ‘Correction Deed’
dated 04.01.1991, but the Trial Court refused it on the ground that it
lacked foundation in the plaint averments. The appellant challenged
the said order before the High Court in Writ Petition No. 1559/2017,
but remained unsuccessful as the High Court was also of the opinion
that the document had no foundation in the plaint. 
4. In the above referred circumstances, the plaintiff filed an
application under Order VI Rule 17 of the CPC for amendment of the
plaint, contending that the said deed was mentioned in the list of
documents and that the contesting parties had knowledge about the
said document. It was therefore contended that even in the absence of
pleadings, there is neither an element of surprise nor prejudice to the
defendants. By its order dated 16.09.2021, the Trial Court rejected the
application. The appellant carried the matter to the High Court. The
High Court by the order impugned before us, confirmed the decision
2

## Page 232

taken by the Trial Court for virtually the same reasons as supplied by
the Trial Court.
5. We heard Mr. Padmesh Mishra, learned counsel appearing for
the appellant, and Mr. Madhur Deo, learned counsel appearing for the
Respondent No. 6. 
6. It is evident that there has been a reference to the ‘Correction
Deed’ dated 04.01.2019 even at the time when the documents were
brought on record. The issue related to introducing the “Correction
Deed” loomed large from the time when the plaintiff was called for
examination-in-chief. The attempt to bring the document on record
however failed for the reason that there is no foundation in the plaint
and that mistake was sought to be corrected immediately after the
decision of the High Court on 02.04.2019.
7. It is interesting to note that the High Court in the order impugned
before us noted that the document in question, i.e. the ‘Correction
Deed’ was referred in the list of documents as exhibit 41 dated
01.09.2014. As there were no pleadings in the plaint about the said
document, High Court proceeded on the ground that the appellant
should not be permitted to amend the plaint for not exercising due
diligence and also for not giving reasons for not laying foundation in
3

## Page 233

the plaint. The relevant portion of the High Court judgment is as
follows:-
“8. …On this crucial aspect, it was revealed during the
course of arguments and even fairly submitted by the learned
Advocate for the petitioner that the document of ‘Correction
Deed’ was infact not filed alongwith list of document at Exhibit
4. Although the document of ‘Correction Deed’ was filed on
record before the trial Court, later on vide list of documents at
Exhibit 41 dated 01.09.2014, the fact remains that there are no
pleadings in the plaint about the said document. As such, the
application for amendment filed after commencement of trial
necessarily required the plaintiff to demonstrate due diligence
on his part. A perusal of the application for amendment shows
that there are no reasons mentioned by the plaintiff for not
incorporating pleadings about ‘Correction Deed’ in the plaint.
Primary reason about submission of the document vide list of
documents at Exhibit 4 is not found to be acceptable….”
8.  High Court also rejected the contentions of the plaintiff that the
defendants would not be prejudiced or that they are not taken by
surprise. The further contention that the plaintiff is a rustic and illiterate
person and that the Court must allow the amendment, taking a larger
perspective of the matter was also rejected. 
9. Having considered the matter in detail, we are of the opinion that
the application for amendment has a particular background and it has
to be seen in the context of the list of documents filed on 01.09.2014,
containing the ‘Correction Deed’ at exhibit 41. The appellant also
relied on the said document during the course of examination-in-chief
on 24.11.2016. When the decision of the Trial and High Court in
4

## Page 234

injuncting the appellant from relying on the said document had
become final with the order dated 02.04.2019 in the first round, the
appellant found it rather compelling to file the present application for
amendment of plaint to set right the mistake that had occurred. We
cannot lose sight of the background in which the application came to
be filed, and these are precisely the circumstances in which power
under Order VI Rule 17 of the CPC is to be exercised. There is
certainly some amount of inconvenience caused to the respondents
and it has also delayed the trial, but this can be addressed. 
10. For the reasons stated above, the appeal is allowed, the
judgment and order passed by the High Court is set aside. The
application for amendment of the plaint is allowed subject to the
appellant paying an amount of Rs. 25,000/- (Rupees Twenty Five
Thousand) as costs to the respondents within three weeks from today.

Leave granted. 
2. By the impugned order, an interim order issued by a 
learned Single Judge, was affirmed by the Division Bench. 
The learned Single Judge on a challenge made by the 
respondent herein against an arbitration award, directed 
deposit of 75% of Rs.30,71,386/ - (the claim amount allowed 
in favour of the appellant herein) along with simple interest 
@ 6.5% per annum from 18.09.2010 to 04.07.2025, failing 
which the appeal under Section 34 was liable to be rejected. 
The appeal filed therefrom resulted in the impugned order, 
which affirmed the interim order. 

## Page 238

Page 2 of 6 
 
 
3. We have heard  Ms. Mrinal Kanwar , learned AoR 
appearing for the appellant and Mr. Arjun Amanchi, learned 
Counsel appearing for the respondent. 
4. Learned Counsel for the appellant specifically took us 
to Sections 16 and 19 of the Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises Development Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to 
as ‘the Act of 2006’) to contend that in making a deposit, the 
compound interest with monthly interest at three times of the 
bank rate notified by the Reserve Bank  of India, also has to 
be reckoned to compute the 75% of the total amounts in the 
award. Reliance was placed on  Goodyear India Limited v.  
Norton Intech Rubbers Private Limited and Anr. 1 and 
Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority v. Aska 
Equipments Ltd.2  
5. Learned Counsel for the respondent, however, 
argued that there is a lack of clarification insofar as the 
interest granted, in which circumstances, the appellant 
themselves had approached the Arbitral Tribunal for 
clarification, which was declined by the Arbitral Tr ibunal. It 
 
1 (2012) 6 SCC 345 
2 (2022) 1 SCC 61 

## Page 239

Page 3 of 6 
 
 
was only in the circumstances of such confusion arising from 
the order itself that the High Court, as an interim measure, 
directed deposit of 75% of the award amount along with 6.5% 
simple interest. 
6. Section 16 is a non-obstante clause which gives short 
shrift to the terms of any agreement or any law for the time 
being in force, making the buyer liable to pay compound 
interest with monthly rests to the supplier at three times of 
the bank rate notified by the Reserve Bank  of India. Section 
19 also mandates that any court entertaining an application 
for setting aside a decree, award or order , arising from an 
award made by the Council itself or by any institution 
providing alternative dispute resolution services to which the 
reference is made by the Council, shall not entertain the 
same, unless the supplier ha s deposited 75% of the ' amount 
in terms of the decree, award or as the case may be, the other 
order in the manner directed by such court'. Proviso also 
requires such amounts deposited, to be disbursed to  the 
supplier on such conditions as it is deemed  necessary, 
during the pendency of the application/appeal.  

## Page 240

Page 4 of 6 
 
 
7. There can be no dispute that it is not the claim amount 
alone, which has to be reckoned at the time of computing 
75% and it is the 'amount in the terms of the decree, award or 
any other order in the manner directed by such court'.  
Goodyear India Limited 1 held that under Section 19, the 
Court has no discretion to either waive or reduce the amount 
of 75% of award as a pre -deposit for entertaining the 
application/appeal. The words ' in the manner directed by 
such court ' only enables an order of instalment at the 
discretion of the Court. Gujarat State Disaster Management 
Authority2 also reiterated that the court has no discretion to 
deviate from the condition of pre-deposit of 75% of the award 
amount under Section 19 and that the discretion is only 
insofar as granting instalment. 
8. We also notice the contention raised by the learned 
Counsel for the respondent that there was a confusion in the 
terms of interest as ordered in the award. We have looked at 
the award, and it clearly reads so: -  
‘64. In the result, the counter claims are rejected and 
the Respondent is directed to pay the Claimant a sum 
of Rs. 30,71,386/- (Rupees Thirty Lakhs Seventy One 
Thousand Three Hundred and Eighty Six Only) along 

## Page 241

Page 5 of 6 
 
 
with the compound interest with monthly rests at 
three times the bank rate of 6.50% notified by the 
Reserve Bank of India under Notification No. 
RBI/2024-25/111 DOR.RET.REC.57/ 12/01.001/ 
2024-25 dated 07.02.2025 and as stipulated in 
Section 15 & 16 of the  MSMED Act, 2006 from 
18.09.2010 till the date of realization. No cost.’ 
 
9. There is absolute clarity insofar as the interest having 
been awarded at three times of the bank rate, which at the 
time of award, was notified as 6.5%  by the Reserve Bank of 
India, which also has to be computed with monthly rests. 
Hence, the interest has to be calculated @ 19.5% per annum 
with compound interest at monthly rests. 
10. Neither can it be said that there was lack of clarity nor 
can it be said that interim order passed by the learned Single 
Judge, as affirmed by the Division Bench, is valid in law. On 
the clear statutory mandate, 75% of the amount awarded 
should include the claim allowed and the interest awarded.  
11. The respondent who is applicant before the High 
Court shall calculate the interest @ 19.5%, computed on a 
compounded basis with monthly rests and pay 75% of the 
same, after deducting the simple interest @ 6.5% already 

## Page 242

Page 6 of 6 
 
 
deposited, within a period of two months from today. Till such 
time, the application under Section 34 shall stand deferred. 
Insofar as the amounts already deposited, the appellant 
would be entitled to seek for disbursal of the same on such 
conditions as the Court may direct. On the further deposit 
also, the said amount s can be disbursed, again on such 
conditions as determined by the Court; ensuring security to 
facilitate refund if the claim or any part of it is rejected. 
12. The appeal is allowed without any observations on the 
merits of the matter which shall be considered by the High 
Court after hearing both parties, if the deposit as directed 
herein is made, or else application under Section 34 shall 
stand rejected. 
13. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

Committee (SLAC), and that committee in its meeting held on

6. Convict No. 417, P. K. Azeez, the petitioner, has been
found guilty in two separate murder cases and is presently
undergoing sentence. While serving his sentence for the
murder of two persons, he was released on ordinary leave,
during which he absconded for more than four years without
returning to prison and committed another murder during the
period of such abscondence. As on 22.09.2025, the petitioner
has undergone 34 years, 8 months and 23 days of actual
imprisonment. As per Section 77 of the Kerala Prisons and
Correctional Services (Management) Act, 2010, "well-behaved,
long-term convicted prisoners may be permanently released
with the objective of their reformation and rehabilitation."

that  even  after  undergoing  incarceration  for  such  a

indicate a lack of genuine reformation on the part of the

good conduct contemplated under Section 77 of the Act. In
view of these facts, the application submitted by Convict
No.  417,  P.  K.  Azeez,  of  Central  Prison
& Correctional Home, Viyyur, for premature release is hereby
rejected.

## Page 253

        UPON hearing the counsel the Court made 
the following
                      O R D E R
1. We were appalled by the impugned order in
these Special Leave Petitions, since the accused
in a double murder case were casually released on
bail. After narrating the prosecution case, the
contentions raised by the accused and the vehement
opposition by the Government Advocate, bail was
granted on the following reasoning:
“After  hearing  the  rival  submissions
and  considering  the  fact  that  there
are more than hundred criminal appeals
being listed before this court per day
and  it  is  not  humanly  possible  to
decide  all  on  merit.  There  is  remote
possibility  of  hearing  of  this  appeal
in  near  future  hence  prayer  for  grant
of bail to the applicant is allowed.
Let  the  applicant-appellant  convicted
and  sentenced  in  the  aforesaid  crime
be  released  on  bail  on  his  furnishing
a  personal  bond  and  two  sureties  each
of the like amount to the satisfaction
of court concerned.”
3

## Page 254

2. We are often confronted with such orders,
either granting bail or refusing it without any
consideration at all. We are quite aware that
there are filed, a number of bail applications,
the prevalence of which is seen even in this
Court.  However,  as  Constitutional  Courts,  we
cannot  take  a  callous  or  casual  approach  in
disposing of such applications, be it refusal or
grant. There should be some plausible reason shown
justifying the nature of the disposal of the bail
application. When the applications are rejected,
merely on the seriousness of the offences alleged
without  looking  at  any  of  the  incriminating
circumstances it leads to pre-trial detention,
impinging upon the liberty of the citizen and
adding to the woes of the already overcrowded
prisons. However, neither overcrowded prisons nor
the burden of pendency; which we judges are bound
to carry and deal with, shall result in bail being
granted, when the offence is serious, the offender
is virulent and there is fear in the minds of the
4

## Page 255

victims or their families or the society at large.
3. Here  is  an  offence,  where  just  after
twilight, in a busy area the assailants barged
into a shop and shot two persons to death. The
persons who died are said to be witnesses in
another murder case and the intention was to
prevent their testimony before court. Eyewitness
testimony was believed by the trial court, in
convicting the accused. PW1, PW2 and PW4 spoke of
the incident in graphic detail. Their presence was
found to be natural at the place of occurrence.
The  High  Court  regretfully,  released  the
appellants on bail only on the ground of the large
pendency of criminal appeals in that Court and the
impossibility  to  decide  all  that  on  merits.
Considering the conviction entered into by the
trial court and on a  prima  facie  view of the
incriminating circumstances having been proved,
the High Court could have released the accused, if
at all on stringent conditions especially noticing
5

## Page 256

the fact that they were in custody for 8 years,
more than half of the period, if eventually their
appeal is found devoid of merit and there is
remission applied to their life sentence.
4. Learned  Counsel  for  the  appellant
specifically pointed out that they are unable to
enter into the locality, since the accused, who
are seasoned criminals, are creating a terror
situation. We reiterate that in fact there was a
motive alleged that they had gone on a rampage,
killing two persons; witnesses in another murder
case, so as to silence them. If that be so, the
threat perception raised by the petitioner herein
is amply justified.
5. We hence direct that the accused released on
bail, who are the party respondents herein shall
mark  their  presence  before  the  jurisdictional
Station House Officer every two weeks on Monday,
for the next six months and then once on the
second Monday of the month. Jurisdictional SHO
6

## Page 257

also shall remain alert with respect to the threat
perception spoken of by the petitioner herein and
if there is any such threat levelled or assault
perpetrated or a complaint received, the accused
shall be immediately taken into custody, de-hors
the bail granted by the High Court. The accused
then shall not be released by any court other than
this Court.
6. With  the  above  stringent  conditions,  we
dispose of the Special Leave Petitions.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall also
stand disposed of.
(HARPREET KAUR)                   (POOJA SHARMA)
COURT MASTER (SH)               COURT MASTER (NSH)

SIDDARTH JEPH @ SIDDHARTH JEPH @

                        VERSUS
STATE OF JHARKHAND           RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Heard learned counsel appearing for the parties.
2. Leave granted.
3. The  FIR  being  Airport  P.S.  Case  No.40/2024,
corresponding to S.T. Case No.783/2024, came to be
registered  for  the  offences  punishable  under  Section
1

## Page 272

140(2), 140(3), 61(2) of the  Bharatiya  Nyaya  Sanhita,
2023,  as well as under Section 25(1-B)(a), 26, and 35 of
the Arms Act. The said FIR came to be lodged against one
Sweta Pati and three other unknown persons.
4. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that the
appellant is not named in the FIR; he has been implicated
on the basis of the statement of co-accused. It is further
submitted that the Test Identification Parade was not
conducted by the investigating agency, and in fact, three
other co-accused, including the accused Sweta pati who is
named in the FIR, have been released on bail. Learned
counsel, therefore, urged that on the ground of parity, the
case of the appellant be considered.
5. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent –
State, though opposes the request made by the appellant
for grant of bail, is not in a position to dispute the fact that
three other co-accused, including the accused who is
named in the FIR, have been released on bail.
2

## Page 273

6. Having considered the submissions canvassed by
learned counsel appearing for the parties and having gone
through the material placed on record, it emerges that the
appellant has not been named in the FIR. One Sweta Pati
has been named in the FIR, alongwith three unknown
persons. The appellant has placed on record the copy of
the orders passed by the concerned High Court in the case
of three other co-accused, including Sweta Pati who is
named in the FIR. Copies of the said orders are placed on
record at page Nos.25, 37, and 42 of the compilation. The
appellant is in custody since 30th August 2024. Further, the
Test Identification Parade has not been conducted by the
investigating agency.
7. Looking to the aforesaid facts and circumstances of
the present case, we are of the view that the case of the
appellant for grant of bail deserves consideration.
8. Accordingly, the impugned order dated 23.04.2026
passed by the High Court of Jharkhand at Ranchi in B.A.
No.51/2026   is   set   aside.   Appellant   is   ordered  to  be
3

## Page 274

released on bail on such terms and conditions as may be
imposed by the concerned Trial Court. Appeal is accordingly
allowed.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

O R D E R 
 
1. The present petitions have been filed by the petitioner -
husband seeking transfer of Matrimonial Case No. 426 of 
2021, instituted by the respondent -wife, and Matrimonial 
Case No. 73 of 2023, instituted by the petitioner -husband, 
both pending before the Prin cipal Judge, Family Court, 
Patna, Bihar, to the Court of the Principal Judge, Family 
Court, New Delhi. 
2. The facts in brief are as follows:  
2.1 The marriage between the parties was solemnised on 
19th April 2019 in accordance with Hindu rites and 
customs. The parties have been residing separately 
since March 2020. 
2.2 The respondent -wife instituted Matrimonial Case No. 
426 of 2021 seeking dissolution of marriage, which is 
pending before the Family Court, Patna.  

## Page 278

T.P.(C.) Nos.970-971 of 2026  2 
 
2.3 The petitioner -husband thereafter instituted 
Matrimonial Case No. 73 of 2023 seeking restitution of 
conjugal rights. The said proceedings came to be 
transferred from Ranchi to Patna pursuant to the order 
dated 13th December, 2022 passed by this Court in 
Transfer Petition (Civil) No. 307 of 2022. 
2.4 Both parties are presently residing in New Delhi and 
jointly seek transfer of the aforesaid proceedings to 
Delhi. 
3. We have learned counsel for the parties and perused the 
material available on the record.  
4. During the pendency of these petitions, this Court, vide order 
dated 21st  May, 2026, referred the disputes between the 
parties to the Supreme Court Mediation Centre. The parties 
have, pursuant thereto, arrived at a Settlement Agreement 
dated 15th June, 2026. 
5. A joint application, being I.A. No. 216314 of 2026, has been 
filed under Article 142 of the Constitution of India, seeking 
appropriate orders to give effect to the Settlement Agreement, 
including dissolution of the marriage and closure of all 
pending proceedings arising out of the matrimonial dispute. 
6. We have perused the Settlement Agreement and have 
interacted with the parties. They have affirmed before us that 

## Page 279

T.P.(C.) Nos.970-971 of 2026  3 
 
the settlement has been arrived at voluntarily, of their own 
free will and without any coercion, undue influence or fraud. 
They have further stated that there is no possibility of 
reconciliation and have mutually agreed to dissolve their 
marriage. 
7. As per the terms of the Settlement Agreement, the parties 
have agreed to withdraw all proceedings instituted by them 
against each other and have waived all claims towards 
permanent alimony, interim maintenance or any other 
financial support from each other . They have also 
undertaken not to raise any further claims or initiate any 
civil or criminal proceedings against each other in relation to 
the matrimonial dispute. 
8. We are satisfied that the Settlement Agreement has been 
voluntarily executed by the parties and that its terms are 
lawful. Having regard to the amicable resolution of all 
disputes through mediation before the Supreme Court 
Mediation Centre and the unequivo cal desire of the parties 
to bring their matrimonial relationship to an end, we are of 
the considered view that this is a fit case for exercise of the 
plenary powers of this Court under Article 142 of the 
Constitution of India to do complete justice betwee n the 
parties and bring a quietus to all disputes arising out of their 
matrimonial relationship. 

## Page 280

T.P.(C.) Nos.970-971 of 2026  4 
 
9. Accordingly, I.A. No. 216314 of 2026 is allowed. In terms of 
the Settlement Agreement which shall form part of this order 
and in exercise of our powers under Article 142 of the 
Constitution of India, we issue the following directions: 
9.1. The marriage solemnised between the petitioner and 
the respondent on 19th April, 2019 stands dissolved 
by a decree of divorce by mutual consent. 
9.2.  All pending civil and criminal proceedings instituted 
by either party against the other, arising out of or in 
connection with their matrimonial dispute, shall 
stand quashed and shall be deemed to have been 
finally disposed of. This shall include, inter alia: 
(i) Criminal Complaint Case bearing CCC(P) No.1177 
of 2021 pending before the CJM, Patna Sadar, 
Patna, Bihar 
(ii) Matrimonial Case No.426 of 2021 pending before 
Principle Judge, Family Court, Patna, Bihar. 
(iii) Matrimonial Case No.73 of 2023 pending before 
Principle Judge, Family Court, Patna, Bihar. 
10. Both parties, who are present before this Court, have 
affirmed that they shall abide by the terms and conditions of 
the Settlement Agreement and shall not raise any further 

## Page 281

T.P.(C.) Nos.970-971 of 2026  5 
 
claims or initiate any civil or criminal proceedings against 
each other in relation to the matrimonial dispute. 
11. The transfer petitions stand disposed of in the aforesaid 
terms. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of. 
Registry shall communicate this order to all the concerned 
Courts where the matters were pending and have been 
closed by this order. Formal orders may be passed by the 
respective Courts closing the proceedings. The Registry shall 
also draw the decree accordingly.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Criminal Appeal  No(s).      /2026
SLP (Crl.) No(s). 9025/2026
SRINIVAS RAO KAKI                         Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF KARNATAKA                        Respondent(s)
O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This  appeal  arises  from  an  order  dated
27.04.2026 passed by the High Court of Karnataka at
Bengaluru rejecting the regular bail prayer of the
appellant  in  connection  with  FIR  No.  118/2024,
registered at P.S. Seshadripuram Sub-Division, High
Grounds, Bengaluru City.
4. At the outset, it may be put on record that the
appellant had earlier also petitioned this Court for
grant of bail which was rejected  vide order dated
14.02.2025 passed in Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No.
1999/2025.  However,  at  that  point  of  time,  the
1

## Page 284

appellant had suffered incarceration for a period of
about six months only; whereas by now he has remained
in  jail  for  a  period  exceeding  two  years.  The
submission  on  behalf  of  the  appellant  is  that,
admittedly,  the  appellant  is  not  an  employee  or
officer of Valmiki Corporation whose money has been
diverted to various accounts. The charging sections
put against the appellant are of offences where the
maximum  punishment  is  seven  years.  Moreover,  the
charge-sheet indicts 14 accused out of which 12 have
been admitted to bail. In such circumstances, the
appellant is entitled to be released on bail pending
trial.
5.  The learned Counsel for the State- respondent has
opposed the prayer for bail by pointing out that the
appellant  and  the  other  co-accused,  namely,
Satyanarayana Verma, are the main accused who had
conspired  with  the  Managing  Director  of  Valmiki
Corporation for diverting funds of the corporation to
various accounts from which withdrawals were made. He
further submits that it has been discovered that the
appellant was also implicated in a similar case in the
State of Chhattisgarh wherein he was granted bail vide
2

## Page 285

order dated 04.08.2023 passed by the High Court of
Chhattisgarh. He, however, could not dispute that out
of the 14 accused in the present case, 12 have been
granted  bail  and  that  by  now  the  appellant  has
suffered incarceration for a period exceeding two
years.  He  also  could  not  dispute  that  all  the
offences, of which the appellant is accused of, are
punishable with a term sentence not exceeding seven
years.
6.  Having  regard  to  the  aforesaid  submissions
including the fact that by now the appellant has
suffered two years of incarceration pending trial,
without expressing any opinion on the merits of the
case, we are of the view that the appellant, at this
stage, is entitled to be released on bail pending
trial. 
7.  Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The order
passed by the High Court rejecting the regular bail
prayer of the appellant is set aside.
8. The appellant shall be released on bail on such
terms and conditions as the trial court may deem fit
to impose in the facts and circumstances of the case.
Those  conditions  would  include  a  condition  of
3

## Page 286

surrender of passport by the appellant as also that he
shall report at the Police Station concerned where the
First Information Report was registered in the first
week of every month starting from September 2026, and
he shall also disclose his mobile number to the
police. 
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal arises from an order dated
04.02.2026 passed by the High Court of Madhya
Pradesh at Jabalpur by which the application of
the  appellant  for  suspension  of  sentence
awarded  by  the  trial  court,  pending
consideration of his appeal (CRA No. 1640/2021)
has been dismissed.
4.  At the outset, the learned counsel for the
appellant submits that co-accused- Harishankar
Gautam & Mukesh, who are also brothers-in-law
of the deceased, have been granted bail by this
Court after suspending the sentence vide order
dated  28.07.2025  passed  in  Criminal  Appeal
arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 7352/2025. The
order dated 28.07.2025 is extracted below:
“1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the
parties.
1

## Page 290

3. This appeal arises from an
Order passed by the High Court
of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur
rejecting the application of the
appellant seeking suspension of
sentence  pending  his  criminal
appeal.
4. The contention of the learned
counsel  for  the  appellant  is
that though the appellant has
been  convicted  by  the  trial
court, it is a case based on
circumstantial  evidence.  The
appellant was not a resident of
the  house  where  the  deceased
died; in fact he is brother-in-
law of the deceased. The husband
of  the  deceased  is  also  an
accused.  The  deceased  was
married to appellant’s brother
more than 11 years before the
incident and therefore benefit
of  presumption  would  not  be
available  to  the  prosecution.
Additionally, the appellant has,
by now, served over five and
half years of sentence. 5. The
learned  counsel  for  the
respondent-State has opposed the
prayer of bail and has submitted
that this is a case where wife
and children were done to death
2

## Page 291

in a brutal manner and therefore
it  is  not  a  fit  case  for
suspension of sentence.
6. We have considered the rival
submissions and have perused the
materials available on record.
It is not in dispute that the
appellant is brother-in-law of
the  deceased  and  as  per  the
appellant’s case, he had been
residing  separate  from  his
brother.  It  is  also  not  in
dispute that it is a case based
on circumstantial evidence and
no presumption other than one
available under Section 106 of
the Indian Evidence Act, 1872,
if at all available, would be
there for the prosecution.
7. In such circumstances, having
regard to the fact that there is
no  likelihood  of  the  appeal
being heard by the High Court in
near future, we are of the view
that  the  appellant,  having
already served more than five
and half years of sentence, is
entitled to the benefit of bail.
Consequently,  the  appeal  is
allowed.
8. The order of the High Court
rejecting the prayer to suspend
3

## Page 292

the sentence, is set aside. The
sentence  awarded  to  the
appellant is hereby suspended.
The appellant shall be released
on  bail  on  such  terms  and
conditions as the trial court
concerned may deem fit to impose
in the facts and circumstances
of the case.
9. It is made clear that we have
not expressed any opinion on the
merits of the appeal.
10. Pending application(s), if
any, shall stand disposed of.” 
5.  The  learned  Counsel  for  the  State-
respondent has opposed the prayer for bail by
submitting that the case of the appellant is
distinguishable from the other accused in as
much as the house of the appellant adjoins the
house of the deceased and is separated by an
alley. It has also been submitted that the iron
gate between the two houses must have remained
open as carbon particles are found on both
sides of the gate. However, it is not denied
that the husband of the deceased is also an
accused who has been granted bail.
6. Be that as it may, having regard to the
fact that the appellant is brother-in-law of
the  deceased  and  had  a  separate  place  of
residence, and the husband of the deceased is
also an accused, we are of the view that the
4

## Page 293

appellant is entitled to be released on bail
after  suspension  of  sentence  on  ground  of
parity.
7.  Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The
order dated 04.02.2026 passed by the High Court
is set aside. The sentence awarded by the trial
court is hereby suspended pending consideration
of CRA No. 1640/2021 preferred by the appellant
before the High Court.
8. Pending consideration of his appeal, the
appellant shall be released on bail on such
terms and conditions as the trial court may
deem  fit  to  impose  in  the  facts  and
circumstances of the case.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall
stand disposed of.

1. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant,
learned counsel for Respondent No.1-State of Madhya
Pradesh  and  learned  counsel  for  Respondent  No.2-
informant.
2. Leave granted.
3. This appeal takes exception to the order dated
15.06.2026 passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh,
Bench at Indore (briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter),
cancelling  the  anticipatory  bail  granted  to  the
appellant by the Trial Court.
4. Appellant  is  an  accused  in  Crime  No.97/2025
registered at Police Station- MIG, District- Indore,
Madhya Pradesh under Sections 420, 406, 408, 467, 471
and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short,
‘IPC’).
1

## Page 296

5. The Trial Court vide the order dated 18.03.2025,
granted anticipatory bail to the appellant. Relevant
portion of order dated 18.03.2025 reads thus:
“From the Case Diary of Crime No. 97/2025 of
Police Station M.I.G., Indore, it is evident that
the investigation in the case is almost complete.
Furthermore, the entire case is primarily based on
documentary evidence, which is predominantly under
the control of the prosecution. In this case, the
anticipatory  bail  applications  of  the  other
accused persons, Smt. Akanksha and Smt Kavita,
have already been granted by this Court on 10-03-
2025. There is no possibility of the present
Applicant/Accused tampering with the evidence in
the case, since the entire case is wholly based on
documentary evidence. In such circumstances, there
is no possibility of any new evidence coming to
light  in  favour  of  the  State  Government  by
arresting  the  present  Applicant/Accused  Rahul
Arora. Therefore, without going into the merits
and demerits of the case, the First Anticipatory
Bail  Application  filed  on  behalf  of  the
Applicant/Accused Rahul, son of Prem Arora, under
Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha
Sanhita, is hereby allowed, and it is directed
that if he is arrested by Police Station M.I.G. in
the present crime, he shall be released on bail
upon  furnishing  a  personal  bond  of  50,000/-₹
(Rupees Fifty Thousand) and a surety bond of the
same amount.
In addition, the following conditions are imposed
upon the Anticipatory Bail Applicant under Section
438(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973:
(a) The Anticipatory Bail Applicant shall make
himself  available  whenever  required  to  answer
questions put by the police officer.
(b) The Applicant/Accused shall not, directly or
2

## Page 297

indirectly,  give  any  inducement,  threat,  or
promise to any person acquainted with the facts of
the case so as to dissuade him from disclosing
such facts to the police or the Court.
(c) The Anticipatory Bail Applicant shall not
leave India without the permission of the Court.
(d) The Anticipatory Bail Applicant shall strictly
comply with Section 437(3) of the CrPC, 1973.”
6. Respondent No.2-informant assailed this order of
anticipatory bail before the High Court and vide order
dated 15.06.2026, the anticipatory bail granted to the
appellant was cancelled.
7. This Court, by order dated 30.06.2026, had issued
notice and stayed the order of the High Court dated
15.06.2026  cancelling  the  anticipatory  bail  of  the
appellant.
8. Respondent No.1-State of Madhya Pradesh as well as
Respondent  No.2-informant  have  filed  counter
affidavit(s).
9. We find that till date, there is no allegation or
complaint  that  appellant  has  misused  the  liberty
granted to him.
10. As noticed by the Trial Court, it is a matter of
documentary evidence and custodial interrogation of the
appellant is not required.
11. In our view, the High Court erred in cancelling the
anticipatory bail granted to the appellant. Bail once
3

## Page 298

granted,  regular  or  anticipatory,  should  not  be
interfered with lightly.
12. We, therefore, set aside the impugned order dated
15.06.2026 passed by the High Court and restore the
anticipatory  bail  granted  by  the  Trial  Court  on
18.03.2025 with the conditions mentioned therein.
13. Consequently, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
14. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

Leave granted.
2. Being aggrieved by the order dated 15.12.2025, the
appellants are before this Court in this appeal. By the
said  order,  the  Criminal  Miscellaneous  Writ  Petition
preferred  by  the  appellants  was  dismissed  for  non-
prosecution  and  consequently,  the  interim  order  stood
vacated.
3. Learned senior counsel appearing for the appellants
submitted that merely because the learned counsel for the
appellants was not present before the Court on the fateful
day, their Criminal Miscellaneous Writ Petition seeking
quashing of FIR No.250/2023 and proceedings consequent
thereto was dismissed, as a result the interim order stood
vacated and the criminal proceedings would have continued
but for the interim order granted by this Court.
4. Learned senior counsel also submitted that there has
been a Memorandum of Understanding(MoU) between the parties
under which a sum of Rs.43,00,000/- has been paid by the
appellants. In the circumstances, this Court may consider

## Page 308

2
restoration  of  Criminal  Miscellaneous  Writ  Petition
No.2702/2024 on the file of the High Court and the High
Court may dispose of the said petition by bearing in mind
the MoU arrived at between the parties and which has also
been acted upon by the appellants herein inasmuch as a sum
of Rs.43,00,000/- has been paid by them to respondent No.4
and his associates.
5. Per contra, learned senior counsel appearing for the
respondent-complainant contended that the High Court was
justified  in  passing  the  impugned  order  since  the
appellants herein had sought for quashing of FIR and other
proceedings but did not bother to appear before the Court
on 15.12.2025. The High Court had no other option but to
dismiss  the  Criminal  Miscellaneous  Writ  Petition
No.2702/2024 for non-prosecution and consequently, vacated
the interim order. There is no merit in this appeal and
hence, the same may be dismissed.
6. We have taken note of the submissions advanced at the
bar and we have perused the interim order. The Division
Bench  of  the  High  Court  dismissed  the  Criminal
Miscellaneous Writ Petition No.2702/2024 preferred by the
appellants for non-prosecution solely on account of the
absence  of  the  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
appellants  herein  merely  because  the  counsel  was  not
present in Court. We find that the appellants could not
have suffered in their litigation. The dismissal of the
said Writ Petition for non-prosecution on the criminal

## Page 309

3
side would not also entail recalling of such an order. It
is in the above circumstances, the appellants are before
this Court.
7. We find that the interests of justice would be served
if the appellants are given another opportunity to have
their  Criminal  Miscellaneous  Writ  Petition  heard  on
merits. We say so particularly for the reason that there
has been a MoU arrived at between the parties and it is
stated at the bar that a sum of Rs.43,00,000/- has been
paid  by  the  appellants  herein  to  the  respondent-
complainant.
8. In the circumstances, we set aside the impugned
order. We restore Criminal Miscellaneous Writ Petition
No.2702/2024 on the file of the High Court. The Division
Bench of the High Court is requested to rehear the said
Writ Petition on merits.
9. Consequently, the interim order of the High Court
stands restored till the disposal of the said Writ Petition
by the High Court. 
10. It is needless to observe that the High Court shall
now dispose of the Criminal Miscellaneous Writ Petition
having regard to the circumstances of this case and in
accordance with law.
11. The interim order passed by this Court on 16.03.2026
shall be continued till the disposal of the said Writ
Petition by the High Court.

sought for transfer of the aforesaid proceedings to the Family Court,
Kolkata, West Bengal.
6. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
7. We are satisfied, having regard to the inconvenience the
petitioner is likely to face if the proceedings were continued before
the Family Court, Vadodara, Gujarat, which is at a distance of around
2000 kms from her present place of residence,  that interest of
justice demands grant of the prayer for transfer. That apart, other
proceedings are also pending in the court at Kolkata, West Bengal.
8. Hence, the transfer petition is allowed. FSUIT No.1206 of 2025
titled “Ambrish Dhupelia  vs. Mrs. Rohini  Sethi”  pending before the
Family Court, Vadodara, Gujarat  is transferred to the Family Court,
2

## Page 315

Kolkata, West Bengal.  Records of FSUIT No.1206 of 2025 be
transferred to the transferee court immediately.
9. To avoid delay, the parties are directed to appear before the
transferee court on 13th August, 2026. If any or both the parties fail
to appear on that day, the presiding officer of the transferee court
will fix another date of appearance. Thereafter, he shall be free to
proceed in accordance with law.
10. Notwithstanding that mediation has failed, the presiding officer
of the transferee court shall endeavour to bring about a settlement
between the parties through the process of mediation. If the process
is unsuccessful once again, nothing shall preclude the presiding
officer to take the proceedings to its logical conclusion on its merits
and in accordance with law.
11. If the respondent is unable to attend the proceedings in person
on any occasion, he will be at liberty to seek permission to attend
through the virtual mode and if such a permission is sought, the
presiding officer of the court may proceed to consider it reasonably.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Applications for permission to file Special Leave Petitions
are allowed.
2. These Special Leave Petitions pertain to the elections to the
Delhi State Bar Council, which came to be filed when the election
4

## Page 323

process was nearing completion. During the pendency of these
proceedings, the election process concluded, and counting of the
votes was permitted by this Court with the condition that the
result shall not be declared.
3. Meanwhile, a series of petitions raising grievances against
the conduct of elections in various other State Bar Councils were
also filed. In order to provide an independent, fair and impartial
platform where the questions of fact could also be effectively
resolved, this Court  vide order dated 18.05.2026 (in W.P. (C)
No.589/2026), constituted two Election Tribunals headed by former
Judges of this Court to hear election disputes pertaining to the
various State Bar Council elections. Other State Bar Councils have
already been relegated to the said Election Tribunals. That being
so, we see no reason to take a different view in these cases also.
The instant petitions are, accordingly, disposed of with liberty to
the aggrieved persons to file their respective petitions before the
Election Tribunals, including those constituted by this Court.
4. Having regard to the fact that the uncertainty regarding the
Bar Council elections ought to come to an end at the earliest, we
request the Tribunal(s), before whom such petitions are listed, to
provide an expeditious hearing, subject to cooperation by all
concerned. It will be highly appreciated if the petitions are
decided within three months.
5. We direct the Bar Council of Delhi to preserve the entire
record, including the original CCTV footage and the videography
recordings and produce the same before the Tribunal(s).
6. Meanwhile, the results will be declared, but the same shall be
5

## Page 324

subject to the outcome of the petitions before the Tribunal(s).
7. It is clarified that we have not expressed any opinion on the
merits of the case.
8. The Delhi Police is also directed to preserve the original
CCTV footage and provide a copy thereof to the Delhi State Bar
Council.
9. The Special Leave Petitions stand disposed of, with pending
application(s), if any.

NARESH DILAWARI ..... APPELLANT(S)

CHARANJIT SINGH OBEROI ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard appellant-in-person and learned counsel for the
Bar Council of Punjab and Haryana as well as Assistant Solicitor
General of India representing the Central Bureau of Investigation
(for short, ‘CBI’).
3. Pursuant to a compliant lodged against the appellant-in-
person, the Bar Council of Punjab and Haryana vide the order dated
20.12.2021, suspended  the  license  (right  to  practice  of  the
appellant-in-person)  for  a  period  of  2  years  against  which
appellant-in-person preferred an appeal before the Disciplinary
Committee of the Bar Council of India being DC Appeal No.1 of 2022.
The Disciplinary Committee passed an order on 16.01.2025 to the
effect that the Bar Council of Punjab and Haryana should verify the
genuineness of the educational qualification of the appellant-in-
person by holding an enquiry and till conclusion of the enquiry,
suspended his license.
4. Be it stated that the appellant-in-person is an advocate by
profession since the year 2001, having obtained his license to
1

## Page 331

practice from the Bar Council of Punjab and Haryana.
5. This order dated 16.01.2025 has been challenged in the present
proceedings.
6. On 15.09.2025, we directed the CBI to investigate whether the
degree obtained by the appellant-in-person is genuine or forged.
Pursuant thereto, CBI has filed a status report in a sealed cover
which we have opened in Court. As per report of the CBI, prima
facie, commission of cognizable offences of forgery, fabrication of
public documents etc., have been made out against the appellant-in-
person and other unknown persons.
7. In the hearing today, learned counsel for the Bar Council of
Punjab and Haryana has produced before us a copy of notification
dated 05.08.2025 disclosing therein that pursuant to direction of
the Disciplinary Committee of the Bar Council of India, enquiry was
carried out by the Bar Council of Punjab and Haryana, which
thereafter submitted Inquiry Report on 11.06.2025. On a direction
by the Disciplinary Committee of the Bar Council of India dated
06.07.2025, the name of the appellant-in-person has been removed
from the Roll of the Bar Council of Punjab and Haryana with further
direction to surrender his license etc.
8. Appellant-in-person submits that the Disciplinary Committee of
the Bar Council of India has exceeded its jurisdiction by directing
the Bar Council of Punjab and Haryana to conduct fresh enquiry,
further directing the Bar Council of Punjab and Haryana to remove
the name of the appellant-in-person from the roll of the Bar
Council. This, he submits, is clearly in excess of jurisdiction.
9. Without expressing any opinion on merit, we are of the view
2

## Page 332

that appellant-in-person may assail the legality and validity of
the notification dated 05.08.2025 in an appropriate proceeding
before the appropriate forum. If the same is filed within a period
of 30 days from today, the question of limitation shall not come in
the way to decide such a challenge. All contentions on behalf of
the appellant-in-person are kept open.
10. Appeal is accordingly disposed of.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
