1. Leave Granted. 
2. The appellant assails cancellation of his regular bail by 
the High Court eight years after the same was granted by 
Additional Sessions Judge, City Civil & Sessions Court, 
Ahmedabad, in connection with FIR No.8/2005 registered at 
CID Crime Police Station, Gandhinagar zone, Gandhinagar 
for the offence punishable under Sections 409, 467, 468, 
420, 406, 471 and 120B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and 
Sections 13(1)(d) & 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption 
Act, 1988.  
3. The appellant is accused of participating in a conspiracy 
to dishonestly avail Rs. 10,00,00,000/- (Rupees Ten crore 
only) loan from the complainant bank , by providing a  
fraudulent security for the same. Specifically, the 
appellant along with the four co-accused partners of the 
same firm availed the aforesaid loan amount by mortgaging 
properties which were already sold by them. The Respondent 
bank has already initiated numerous civil proceedings 
including execution for recovering the aforesaid  loan 
amount.  
4. The trial court granted bail on 17.2.2018, while the 
Chargesheet itself was filed on 3.11.2018. Obviously, the 

## Page 341

2 
 
investigation was complete, and the police did not require 
the custody of the appellant. It is also pertinent that 
the trial is pending for the last eight years and there 
would be no useful purpose served by taking the accused 
back into custody. Considering that the appellant is a 67-
year-old man and has not violated any condition imposed 
upon him for grant of bail in the eight years that he was 
enlarged on bail by the learned trial court, we are of the 
opinion that the appellant can continue on bail. The 
accused shall continue on bail, on the conditions imposed 
by the trial court since the accused was enlarged on bail 
till it was cancelled by the High Court, and the same was 
stayed in the SLP by our interim order, hence the appellant 
is still on bail. 
5. The judgement and order of the Gujarat High Court dated 
08.05.2026 in Cri. Misc. Application No. 14234/2019 is 
hereby set aside.     
6. With the above directions, the appeals stand disposed of.  
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed 
of.

1) Leave granted.
2) The appellant has been enlarged on bail in connection
with C.R. No. 222 of 2019 registered at Police Station
Bhusawal City, District Jalgaon, Maharashtra for the offences
punishable under Sections 302, 307, 120-B, 397 read with
Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘the
IPC’); Sections 3/27 and 4/25 of the Arms Act, 1959; Section
3(2)(v)  of  the  Scheduled  Castes  and  Scheduled  Tribes
(Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 and Section 37(1)(3) read
with Section 135 of the Maharashtra Police Act, 1951.  The
High Court of Judicature at Bombay, vide  the impugned order,
rejected the application for modification of the condition
imposed while granting bail to the appellant vide  its order
dated 07.10.2024.  Aggrieved, the appellant is before us.
1

## Page 346

3) We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the
parties.
4) The limited prayer sought for in Criminal Application No.
389 of 2026 before the High Court, which has been dismissed
and has been impugned in the present appeal, is with respect
to the relaxation of the condition imposed in paragraph 17 of
the  order  dated  07.10.2024  passed  by  the  High  Court.
Paragraph 17 is reproduced as under: 
“17. Appellant shall not enter Bhusawal town
till conclusion of trial, except on the dates on
which his presence is essential for sessions trial.
Appellant shall not tamper prosecution evidence.”
5) On perusal of the counter affidavit filed by the learned
counsel  for  the  respondent,  we  do  not  find  any  serious
objection, except by stating that two more eyewitnesses are
yet to be examined. 
6) In view of the same, we deem it appropriate to set aside
the aforesaid condition imposed by the High Court in the order
granting bail, dated 07.10.2024, and accordingly, allow the
present appeal.

condition  mentioned  in  paragraph  17  of  the  order  dated

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Criminal Appeal No(s).      /2026
SLP (Crl.) No(s). 4108/2026
BIRJU BARMAN                                       Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH                            Respondent(s)
O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal arises from an order dated 29.04.2025
passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur in
Criminal Appeal No. 8350/2023 by which the High Court
dismissed the appeal of the appellant and affirmed the
judgment and order of the Trial Court.
4. The appellant has been convicted under Section 324
of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (“IPC”) and sentenced to
three years R.I. coupled with fine of Rs.1000/-.
5. The Trial Court had acquitted the appellant of the
charge of offences punishable under Section 326 of the IPC
and Section 25(1-B)(b) of the Arms Act, 1959.
6. The submission on behalf of the appellant is that
1

## Page 371

though he has been convicted under Section 324 IPC but
there was no justification for the court to impose maximum
permissible sentence of three years. It has been submitted
that the incident occurred after altercation and scuffle;
therefore, since there was no premeditated intention on
the part of the appellant to cause any serious injury, it
was a fit case where the sentence could have been reduced.
It has also been submitted that as per the custody
certificate issued on 02.12.2025, up to 30.11.2025, the
appellant had spent 1 year 4 months and 6 days in jail,
serving out the sentence, and by now it would be about 2
years. In such circumstances, it has been submitted that
the sentence may be reduced to the period of sentence
undergone by the appellant.
7. The learned counsel for the State-respondent has
opposed the aforesaid prayer by inviting our attention to
paragraph 17 of the impugned judgment wherein the nature
of the injury caused by the appellant has been described.
It is submitted that as per the medical evidence, the
omentum inside the abdomen was found cut and, therefore,
the  injury  could  be  considered  grievous  in  nature,
warranting conviction under Section 326 IPC.
8. We have accorded due consideration to the rival
submissions.
2

## Page 372

9. It  is  not  in  issue  that  no  appeal  has  been
preferred either by the State or by the complainant/
victim for altering the conviction from one under Section
324 IPC to Section 326 IPC.
10. In  such  circumstances,  we  cannot  alter  the
conviction of the appellant from Section 324 IPC to
Section 326 IPC on an appeal preferred by him as it is
well-settled that the appellant cannot be placed in a
position worse than what he would have been if he had not
preferred an appeal.
11. In such circumstances, we would have to consider
whether the maximum sentence awardable under Section 324
IPC was justified in the facts and circumstances of the
case.
12. Having regard to the facts of the case and by
taking into consideration the nature of the incident,
which  occurred  in  the  heat  of  the  moment  after  an
altercation and scuffle, we are of the view that ends of
justice would be served if the sentence is reduced to the
period of sentence already served by the appellant.
13. Accordingly, the appeal is partly allowed. The
conviction of the appellant under Section 324 IPC is
affirmed. However, the sentence is reduced to the period
of sentence already served by the appellant.
3

## Page 373

14. The appellant shall be released forthwith subject
to deposit of Rs.1,000/- fine imposed by the Trial Court,
unless he is wanted in any other case.
15. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

the appellant is entitled to bail. Besides, the
appellant has remained in jail for a period of about
one year nine months pending trial.

5. On conclusion of the investigation chargesheet has been filed. It is to be

investigating agency found no sufficient evidence against other four family
members and chargesheeted only the appellant (husband of the deceased).
There are 26 prosecution witnesses and on framing of the charge, five
prosecution witnesses have been examined including the complainant.
Subsequently an application under Section 319 CrPC has been moved to
arraign the other family members, against whom chargesheet had not been
filed, to be brought on record as accused and said application is said to have

examined only after evaluating the entire evidence that would be tendered

apprehension of the prosecution.

bail.
(SLP (Crl.)  No.  14429/2026)                             1

## Page 386

5. Based on a secret information the police officials
reached the house situated adjacent to the agricultural
land of the appellant’s father on 06.02.2025 where the
appellant was found sleeping and on conducting a search
they found 84.42 kgs of poppy husk recovered from a
storage area where the fodder was kept. Hence, he was
taken into custody on the same day and he is in judicial
custody for the past one year six months. As noticed from
the chargesheet the role attributed to the appellant is
being in conscious possession of 84.42 kgs of poppy husk.
6. Subsequent to the filing of the chargesheet the
jurisdictional Court has taken cognizance and has also
framed the charges on 04.09.2025 and despite several
months the trial has not progressed or in other words the
proceedings are going on at a snail’s pace.
7. Having regard to the fact that delay is not
attributable to the accused and also the fact that there are
no antecedents against the appellant and the fact that he
is in judicial custody for the last one year six months would
persuade us to accept his prayer for grant of bail.
(SLP (Crl.)  No.  14429/2026)                             2

## Page 387

8. Hence, we allow this appeal, set aside the impugned
order and direct the appellant to be released on bail on
such terms and conditions as the jurisdictional Court may
deems fit to impose.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned counsel for the respondent-State of Chhattisgarh.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by the order dated 10.03.2026
passed by the High Court of Chhattisgarh (briefly the
‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the regular bail
application of the appellant.
4. Appellant  is  an  accused  in  Crime  No.527/2025
registered at Police Station- Gandhi Nagar, Ambikapur,
District- Sarguja, Chhattisgarh under Sections 137(2) and
103(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (for short,
‘BNS’).
5. This Court vide order dated 24.07.2026 had issued
notice pursuant to which respondent-State of Chhattisgarh
has filed counter affidavit.
1

## Page 396

6. Allegation against the appellant is that he had
committed  murder  of  the  deceased  girl  following
celebration of his birthday party. The victim went missing
from 04.08.2025 but her mortal remains were recovered on
11.11.2025.
7. At the time of commission of the alleged offence,
appellant was below 18 years of age, though he has now
crossed the threshold of 18 years.
8. Bail application of the appellant was denied by the
Juvenile Justice Board against which appellant preferred
an  appeal  which  was  also  rejected  by  the  Children
Court/Additional Sessions Judge, Fast Track Special Court
(POCSO Act), Sarguja, Ambikapur. Thereafter, appellant
preferred a revision petition under Section 102 of the
Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act,
2015 before the High Court. By the impugned order, the
High Court rejected the prayer for bail of the appellant
on the following grounds:
“Upon careful consideration of the facts and
circumstances of the case, and from the social
status report it is evident that the applicant
has studied up to Class 9th, left his studies
thereafter, consumes alcohol and it is clear from
the entire record that the offence has been
committed in a pre-planned manner. The applicant
is not under the control of his parents and
granting bail to the applicant at this stage
would  result  in  a  lack  of  proper  care  and
protection,  likely  expose  him  to  moral  and
psychological risks, and compromise the interests
2

## Page 397

of justice. Therefore, I find no grounds to
interfere  with  the  reasoned  findings  of  the
Juvenile Justice Board and the Appellate Court.
The application is dismissed.”
9. Learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  submits  that
appellant was a juvenile on the date of the alleged
incident. He has no criminal antecedent. The social status
report is not adverse to the appellant. Therefore, it is
necessary that he should be tried as a juvenile. In any
view of the matter, appellant deserves to be released on
bail, more particularly considering the reasons assigned
by the High Court in denying him bail.
10. Learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of
Chhattisgarh has referred to the counter affidavit filed
by the respondent-State of Chhattisgarh and submits that
the  offence  alleged  is  heinous.  Though  a  juvenile,
appellant needs to be tried as an adult for commission of
the aforesaid offence. He submits that trial has commenced
and, therefore, at this stage, appellant may not be
enlarged on bail.
11. We have perused the materials on record.
12. It is seen that appellant was arrested on 11.11.2025
and since then, he has been in custody. There is no
dispute that on the date of commission of the alleged
offence,  appellant  was  a  juvenile.  From  the  counter
affidavit, we find that though the trial has commenced,
only one witness has been examined till date though
3

## Page 398

prosecution has cited 24 witnesses. It appears that the
trial could take some time for its conclusion.
13. In such circumstances and having regard to the fact
that appellant was a juvenile on the date of the alleged
incident, we are inclined to grant bail to the appellant.
14. Having regard to the above,  the impugned order dated
10.03.2026  passed  by  the  High  Court  is  set  aside.
Consequently,  we  direct  that  the  appellant  shall  be
produced before the concerned Trial Court within a maximum
period of 07 days from today, whereafter he shall be
released on bail on such terms and conditions as may be
deemed appropriate.
15. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
16. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

imposing of cost at Rs. 5,00,000/- on both the accused/appellants. The High
Court while quashing the First Information Report (“for short FIR”) it has been
noticed that complainant who is appellant in [SLP (Crl) No. 7394/2026] i.e.,  the
wife of Major Singh and he was suffering from ill health and as such she was
finding difficulty in maintaining the household expenditure and was also
mentally disturbed and the appellant in [SLP (Crl) No. 3452/2026] who was a
Sub-Inspector of Police in Barnala, Punjab whose sister was married in Ludhiana
and as such he used to visit Ludhiana quite often and during such visits she is
said to have got acquainted with him and shared her difficulties and taking
advantage of the situation that she was placed, Sukhwinder Singh is said to
have tricked her to have physical relationship with him and continued the same
for about 15 years. In 2022 she is said to have become pregnant and had her
forceful abortion.
4. Since, the appellant in [SLP (Crl) No. 3452/2026] viz., Sukhwinder
1

## Page 401

Singh was said to be threatening her and blackmailing the complainant, she
lodged a complaint in September, 2022 which resulted in FIR being registered
on 04.01.2023 under Sections 376, 313 and 506 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
(“for short IPC”)  against him and subsequently, in the month of April, 2023 i.e.,
09.04.2023 she is said to have moved an application stating that she was under
depression and her complaint against the appellant in [SLP (Crl) No. 3452/2026]
was not having any truth and she expressed her intention not to prosecute her
complaint.
5. Based on the same, accused had filed a petition under Section 482
for quashing of the proceedings and the Hon’ble High Court while acceding to
his prayer and quashing the FIR had observed as under:
“6. The present petition needs special attention as after lodging of
the FIR, the parties have compromised the matter and an affidavit
has been filed by the complainant that she was under depression
and there is no dearth of truth in the allegations leveled by her in
the FIR. Moreover, the conduct of the petitioner also does not seem
to be above board for the reason that he being a member of Police
force, who is entrusted with the duty to maintain law and order,
peace and harmony in the society, indulged himself in extra-marital
relations by abusing his position and stature. Therefore, the conduct
of the petitioner and the complainant reflect complete disregard for
truth,  morality  and  civilized  societal  values.  Particularly,  the
complainant who initially by lodging false complaints of leveling
serious  allegations  against  the  petitioner,  subsequently,
compromised the matter and demeans the status of other women in
the society and has also made a mockery of legal process and
attempted to exploit the system by dragging the petitioner into
unwarranted criminal proceedings. This conduct of the complainant
is shocking for which the State is directed to take appropriate steps
and initiate criminal proceedings against the  complainant for
abusing the process of law and ruining the life of the petitioner as
well. The financial status of the complainant should also be checked
to verify whether the lodging of present FIR was an abuse of process
of law to enrich herself by putting the integrity of the petitioner at
peril. Considering the facts of the present matter, it is a fit case
where the petitioner as well as the respondent No. 2 should be
burdened with heavy costs.
7. In light of the above, the present petition is disposed of. FIR No.01
dated 04.01.2023, under Sections 376, 313 and 506 of the Indian

subsequent proceedings arising therefrom, are hereby quashed qua

FIR. The cost be deposited within three months from today in the
following account:
Punjab State Legal Services Authority Disaster Relief Fund.
Account No. 44426937384
IFSC SBIN0014656
Bank Name -State Bank of India, Sector 68, SAS Nagar.”

O R D E R
1. These appeals are directed against the order dated 04.08.2025
passed by the National Green Tribunal, Central Zone, Bhopal (NGT)
as well as against the order dated 07.01.2026, dismissing the
appellant’s review petition against the order dated 04.08.2025. The
appellant is a mining proponent involved in the mining and crushing
of masonry stones in the mines situated in Gorir Modi Village,
District Neem Ka Thana, Rajasthan. It seems that respondent No.4
filed an Original Application (OA) No.30/2025 (CZ) before the NGT
without  impleading  the  appellant  as  a  party  respondent.  The
inspection committee was appointed by the Tribunal in the said OA
and when the inspection of the appellant’s premises was carried
out, the appellant came to know of the said OA. The appellant
thereafter joined the proceedings but, seemingly, could not file an
effective defence before the Tribunal. Ultimately, the OA was
allowed against the appellant, which prompted it to file a review
petition, which has also been dismissed by the subsequent order on
the ground that the appellant was not a party to the OA.  
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties. It seems to us
that, in the interest of justice, one opportunity can be granted to
the appellant to file its written statement/counter affidavit/plea
1

## Page 406

of defence, followed by an adequate opportunity of hearing to both
sides by the Tribunal.  
3. Consequently, we allow the appeals in part, set aside the
impugned order dated 04.08.2025 as well as the subsequent review
order dated 07.01.2026. The learned Tribunal shall pass appropriate
orders after hearing the parties.
4. It is clarified that we have not expressed any opinion on the
merits of the case.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Civil) No. 22468 of 2026)
BICKY KUMAR MAHATO APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA & ANR.     RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The present Special Leave Petition arises out of the
order dated 19.03.2026 passed by the High Court of Delhi at
New Delhi in W.P. (C) No. 3494 of 2026, whereby the High
Court declined to entertain the writ petition preferred by
the  appellant  on  the  ground  of  lack  of  t erritorial
jurisdiction.
3. Learned counsel appearing for the appellant submits
that the advertisement in question was issued from Delhi.
It is further submitted that the power to order a fresh
medical examination/medical board vests with the Director
General, CRPF, New Delhi. In these circumstances, the
appellant had preferred the writ petition before the Delhi
High Court.
4. It is submitted that although the matter relates to
the  selection  of  a  Constable  and  the  appellant  is  a

## Page 411

2
resident of Bardhaman, West Bengal, the aforesaid fact
confer jurisdiction upon the Delhi High Court.
5. Learned counsel for the appellant, at the outset,
has drawn the attention of this Court to the judgment
delivered by this Court in Baksish Ahmad v. Union of India
& Anr.1, dealing with the issue of territorial jurisdiction.
6. In  Baksish  Ahmad  (supra), the appellant therein
served at Malda, West Bengal, and the proceedings had taken
place outside Delhi. Nevertheless, this Court held that the
Delhi High Court had jurisdiction under Article 226(1) of
the Constitution of India, inter alia, having regard to the
fact that the headquarters of the concerned Central Armed
Police Force and the relevant central authorities were
situated in Delhi.
7. In the present case also, the headquarters of the
CRPF and the office of the Director General, CRPF, are
situated in New Delhi. The power to order a fresh medical
board is also stated to vest with the Director General,
CRPF, New Delhi.
8. In view of the aforesaid judgment of this Court in
Baksish  Ahmad (supra), we are of the view that the Delhi
High Court has territorial jurisdiction to entertain the
writ petition filed by the appellant. Consequently, the
impugned order dated 19.03.2026 passed by the High Court of
Delhi at New Delhi in W.P. (C) No. 3494 of 2026 is set
1 2026 INSC 630

## Page 412

3
aside.
9. The matter is remanded back to the High Court of
Delhi  for  consideration  and  adjudication  of  the  writ
petition on its merits and in accordance with law.
10. With  the  aforesaid  observations,  the  Appeal  is
allowed. 
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and consequently sentenced
to life imprisonment. The appellant, along with Nagaraj,
filed Criminal Appeal (MD) No.332/2013, which came to be
dismissed by the Madurai Bench of the Madras High Court,
1

## Page 426

vide the impugned judgement dated 25.02.2015.
4. The co-accused, Nagaraj, challenged that judgment of
the  High  Court  before  this  Court  in  SLP  (Crl.)
No.9697/2019 (Criminal Appeal No.1365/2022), which was
finally allowed by a two-Judge Bench, including one of
us (Surya Kant, J., as he then was), vide order dated
19.08.2022. Consequently, Nagaraj stood acquitted.
5. While allowing the appeal of Nagaraj, this Court
relied upon yet another previous order dated 30.01.2019
passed in Criminal Appeal Nos.198/2019 and 199/2019,
whereby the appeals of the co-accused persons, namely,
accused nos.3 and 4 were allowed by this Court, and they
were acquitted.
6. The role attributed to the appellant herein is
similar to the one attributed to Nagaraj, whose appeal
has already been allowed by this Court on 19.08.2022.
This  fact  has  been  fairly  acknowledged  by  learned
counsel for the State. 
7. For the reasons aforestated, we allow this appeal
and set aside the judgment and order of the Trial Court
as well as the impugned judgment of the High Court.
Consequently, the appellant is acquitted of the charges

TRANSFER PETITION (C) NO.1782/2026
VIDYA @ INDRAKALABAI THAKRE                       PETITIONER
                                         VERSUS
VISHVESHWAR THAKRE                         RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Read the office report dated 13th August, 2026.
2. Despite service of notice of this transfer petition under Section
25  of  the  Code  of  Civil  Procedure,  1908  presented  by  Vidya  @
Indrakalabai Thakre (hereafter the petitioner) on Vishveshwar Thakre
(hereafter the respondent), he has not entered appearance.
3. The marriage between the petitioner and the respondent was
solemnized on 01 st April, 2013 according to Hindu rites and customs.
One girl child was born to the petitioner and the respondent from the
wedlock.  However,  the  parties  have  since  drifted  apart  owing  to
differences arising by and between them.
4. The respondent has instituted proceedings under Section 9 of
the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, bearing RCS H.M. No.34/2026 titled
“Vishveshwar Thakre  Vs.  Vidya  @  Indrakalabai  Thakre ”  which  is
pending  before  the  court  of  the  First  Additional  District  Judge,
1

## Page 456

Waraseoni, District Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh.
5. On the multiple grounds urged in the petition, the petitioner
has sought for transfer of the aforesaid proceedings to the court of
the Principal/Additional Judge, Family Court, Nagpur, Maharashtra.
6. Since  the  respondent  has  not  controverted  the
statements/averments made in the petition, we are of the view that
he has no serious objection to grant of the prayer for transfer.
7. We  are  also  otherwise  satisfied,  having  regard  to  the
inconvenience the petitioner is likely to face if the proceedings were
continued in the Family Court at Waraseoni, District Balaghat, Madhya
Pradesh  that  interest  of  justice  demands  grant  of  the  prayer  for
transfer. 
8. Hence, the transfer petition is allowed. RCS H.M. No.34/2026
titled “Vishveshwar Thakre Vs. Vidya @ Indrakalabai Thakre ” pending
before  the  court  of  the  First  Additional  District  Judge,  Waraseoni,
District Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh  is transferred to  the court of the
Principal/Additional  Judge,  Family  Court,  Nagpur,  Maharashtra .
Records  of  Original  RCS  H.M.  No.34/2026  be  transferred  to  the
transferee court immediately .
9. T o avoid delay, the parties are directed to appear before the
transferee court on 18 th September, 2026. If any or both the parties
fail to appear on that day, the presiding officer of the transferee court
will fix another date of appearance. Thereafter, he shall be free to
proceed in accordance with law. 
10. The  presiding  officer  shall  endeavour  to  bring  about  a
2

## Page 457

settlement between the parties through the process of mediation. If
the  process  is  unsuccessful,  nothing  shall  preclude  the  presiding
officer to take the proceedings to its logical conclusion on its merits
and in accordance with law.
11. If the respondent is unable to attend the proceedings in person
on any occasion, he will be at liberty to seek permission to attend
through  the  virtual  mode  and  if  such  a  permission  is  sought,  the
presiding officer of the court may proceed to consider it reasonably .
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

interpretation of Section 176 of the Haryana Panchayati Raj
Act, 1994, we are inclined to set aside the impugned order

premise that no reasons have been adduced by the high court

before it was predicated.

of this order, particularly, by taking note of the fact
that we are dealing with an election petition for which,
time is a relevant factor.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.    OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) No.5330/2026
MUNAF YUSUFBHAI LAKUM ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF GUJARAT ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 02.12.2025, passed by
the High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad (briefly the ‘High Court’
hereinafter) rejecting the bail application of the appellant.
4. Appellant is an accused in C.R. No.11191048231029 of 2023,
registered before the Sarkhej Police Station, Ahmedabad City under
Sections 8(c), 21(c) and 29 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic
Substances Act, 1985 (briefly the ‘NDPS Act’ hereinafter).
5. Allegation against the appellant is that on the basis of
disclosure statement made by co-accused, he has been arrested as
being the supplier of Mephedrone which is a psycotrophic substance.
It may be mentioned that 101 grams of Mephedrone was recovered from
the person and the two wheeler of the co-accused Mujahid Ali
1

## Page 476

Hussain.
6. Appellant is in custody since 08.06.2024.
7. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that considering the
long incarceration of the appellant, Court may consider enlarging
him on bail. The contraband was not recovered from him. Prosecution
has cited 31 witnesses out of which evidence of only 5 have been
recorded. Therefore, conclusion of the trial will take some time. 
8. Per contra, Ms. Swati Ghildiyal, learned counsel for the
respondent submits that it is the appellant who is the mastermind.
The two wheeler which was being driven by the co-accused, belongs
to the appellant. Though, not under the NDPS Act, appellant has
other  criminal  antecedents  including  under  the  Anti-Social
Activities  (Prevention)  Act.  She  further  submits  that  though
prosecution has cited 31 witnesses, it will prune the list of
witnesses to about 14-15 witnesses, 5 of whom have already been
examined. Therefore, the trial would be concluded in a time bound
manner.
9. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and without
expressing any opinion on merit, we are of the view that having
regard to the fact that appellant is behind bars for more than 2
years now, he may be enlarged on bail. 
10. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned order of the High Court
dated 02.12.2025 and direct that the appellant shall be produced
before the learned Special Court within a maximum period of 7 days
from today whereafter he shall be enlarged on bail on such terms
and conditions as may be deemed appropriate. We further direct that
the appellant shall fully cooperate with the ongoing trial and not
2

## Page 477

seek unnecessary adjournments.
11. Appeal is accordingly allowed.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
......................J.
(UJJAL BHUYAN)
......................J.
(ATUL S. CHANDURKAR)
NEW DELHI;
August 17th, 2026.

DEBDAS HALDAR @ GOUR@ GARU                    Appellant(s)
                       VERSUS
STATE OF WEST BENGAL & ANR.             Respondent(s)
 O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal arises from an order dated 01.12.2025 passed
by the High Court of Calcutta rejecting the application
of the appellant for suspension of sentence pending
consideration of his appeal by the High Court against the
order of conviction and sentence recorded by the Trial
Court.
4. At the outset, learned counsel for the appellant submits
that the Trial Court has convicted and sentenced the
appellant to suffer imprisonment of 10 years R.I. whereas
pending consideration of his appeal including the period
spent in jail during trial, the appellant has already
suffered 8 years of incarceration. 
5. In such circumstances, it is submitted, the sentence
awarded to the appellant by the Trial court be suspended
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.11833/2026
1

## Page 480

pending consideration of his appeal and he be released on
bail otherwise the appeal shall be rendered infructuous.
6. The learned counsel for the State has opposed the prayer
for bail by submitting that there is another case against
the appellant of a similar nature.
7. Be that as it may, it is not in dispute that the
appellant by now has suffered 8 years of sentence as
against 10 years awarded by the Trial Court. In such
circumstances,  it  is  a  fit  case  for  suspension  of
sentence pending consideration of his appeal by the High
Court.
8. Consequently, the appeal is allowed. The order of the
High  Court  rejecting  the  prayer  for  suspension  of
sentence is set aside. The sentence awarded by the Trial
Court shall remain suspended pending consideration of
appellant’s appeal by the High Court.
9. The appellant shall be released on bail on such terms
and conditions as the Trial Court may deem fit to impose
in the facts and circumstances of the case.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

regular bail prayer of the appellant in connection with Crime

(C.G.).
4. The submission on behalf of the appellant is that he is
not  named  in  the  First  Information  Report;  nothing
incriminating has been recovered from his possession or at his
pointing out; and the contraband was recovered from a container
truck not owned by the appellant.  Besides, the confessional
statement of the co-accused, which is the basis of appellant’s
implication has no evidentiary value in view of the decision of
this Court in Tofan Singh versus State of Tamil Nadu,  (2021) 4

SCC 1. Therefore, the appellant is entitled to be released on

the prayer for bail but could not dispute that there was no
incriminating  recovery  from  the  appellant  and  that  his
complicity has come to light basis confessional statement of
the co-accused.
6. Having regard to the above, without expressing any opinion
on merits of the prosecution case, we are of the view that the
appellant is entitled to be released on bail pending trial.
7. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed. The order passed by
the High Court rejecting the bail prayer of the appellant is
set aside.
8. The appellant shall be released on bail on such terms and
conditions as the trial court may deem fit to impose in the
facts and circumstances of the case.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

CORAM : 
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE ARAVIND KUMAR
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE VIPUL M. PANCHOLI
For Petitioner(s) :Dr. Aditya Sondhi, Sr. Adv.
                   Mr. Shivesh Kaushik, Adv.
                   Mr. Abhiraj Ray, Adv.
                   Mr. Aamir Abbas Naqvi, Adv.
                   Ms. Devika Dhawan, Adv.

For Respondent(s) :Mr. Raghenth Basant, Sr. Adv.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard the learned senior counsels appearing for the parties, the
order dated 04.03.2025 was passed on the basis of the Memorandum of
Understanding dated 31.12.2024. The respondent was personally present
before this Court and categorically stated that the settlement had been entered
1

## Page 536

into voluntarily, out of free will and without any force, threat or coercion. Acting
upon such representation, this Court accepted the settlement, recorded
payment of ₹5.34 crores to the respondent and declared that all claims
between the parties stood closed.
2. The MoU itself contemplated a full and final settlement of the
disputes  and  contained  undertakings  that  no  further  civil  or  criminal
proceedings or complaints would be initiated and that the parties would abide
by the settlement and raise no further dispute.
3. Significantly, on 03.03.2025, a day prior to the order of this Court,
the respondent had also handed over ten original cheques and expressly
undertaken on behalf of herself and her mother that neither of them would
pursue any legal action pertaining to those cheques.
4. However, the respondent’s own subsequent pleadings disclose that
even prior thereto, on 01.03.2025, she had lodged a complaint before the police
alleging coercion and blackmail in relation to the return of those very cheques
and the property transaction connected with the settlement. Despite the same,
when she appeared before this Court on 04.03.2025, she did not disclose the
said complaint and instead affirmed that the settlement was voluntary and free
from any force or coercion.
5. The said complaint was thereafter made the basis for registration of
an FIR No. 561/2025 dated 18.04.2025. The FIR itself refers to the return of the
cheques on 03.03.2025 and receipt of ₹5.34 crores pursuant to the settlement
before this Court on 04.03.2025.
6. The subsequent legal notice dated 30.04.2025 further sought
withholding of ₹88 lakhs, together with interest, from the consideration payable
in respect of the very property transaction which had facilitated implementation
2

## Page 537

of the settlement.
7. Thus, the contempt does not rest merely on the filing of a
subsequent FIR. It arises from the cumulative conduct of the respondent in
suppressing a subsisting allegation of coercion while obtaining an order from
this Court on an express representation of voluntariness and finality, accepting
the entire settlement amount, and thereafter reviving the very dispute through
criminal and other proceedings in a manner calculated to frustrate the
settlement.
8. The defence that the alleged loan was an independent transaction
involving the respondent’s mother and Amit Dewan/Swati Singhal does not
answer the respondent’s own conduct. The respondent herself was the
complainant in the FIR and had undertaken before the Court not to pursue
proceedings concerning the cheques, and thereafter invoked the criminal
process on allegations directly connected with their return and the property
transaction underlying the settlement.
9. We are, therefore, satisfied that the respondent’s conduct was
deliberate and amounts to an attempt to overreach the order dated 04.03.2025
passed by this Court and defeat the finality attached to the Court-recorded
settlement. The breach cannot be regarded as technical or inadvertent or has
nothing to do with the settlement agreement recorded by this Court.
10. Hence, we are of the considered view, that prima facie  respondent
has wilfully disobeyed the Order dated 04.03.2025 of this Court and respondent-
contemnor/accused being a lady, we extend one opportunity to her to purge in
the contempt and in what manner the purging in the contempt would be done is
left to her discretion.
3

## Page 538

11. Hence, as a last opportunity three weeks’ time is granted.
12. List on 20.08.2026.
(DEEPANSHU)                                     (AVGV RAMU)

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard.
1

## Page 544

2. Learned counsels appearing for the parties would submit that
against the order/judgment dated 21.04.2026 passed by the High Court
affirming the order/judgment dated 10.02.2026 passed by the Commercial
Court whereunder the petitioner has been directed to deposit a sum of Rs.
6,69,52,278/-(Rs. Six Crore Sixty Nine Lakh Fifty Two Thousand Two Hundred
Seventy Eight only), is on the basis of the reply notice dated 21.09.2024
acknowledging the liability to the said extent and said order is called in
question.
3. Having heard the learned counsels appearing for the parties and on
perusal of the entire records, we notice that parties not being ad idem  on the
Agreement dated 08.08.2017 had resulted in respondent invoking arbitration
clause by issuing notice under Section 21 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act,
1996 which resulted in appointment of arbitrators by the Telangana High Court
by Order dated 10.07.2025 constituting the Arbitral Tribunal. In the meantime,
the respondent herein filed an application/petition under Section 9 of the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 for interim measure at which point of time
there was no Constitution of the Arbitral Tribunal in its entirety. On 10.02.2026
the Commercial Court passed an ex parte  order directing the petitioner herein
to deposit the amount aforestated, the appeal filed challenging the said order
resulted in its dismissal under the impugned order/judgment. Hence, this
petition.
4. Though several contentions have been urged to buttress their
respective arguments, we are of the considered view, that in view of the
Constitution of the Arbitral Tribunal and the parties being before the Tribunal, to
secure the financial interest of the respondent who has had the benefit of the
impugned order, it would suffice to direct the petitioner herein to furnish the
2

## Page 545

bank guarantee for the sum of Rs. 6,69,52,278/-(Rs. Six Crore Sixty Nine Lakh
Fifty Two Thousand Two Hundred Seventy Eight only) within six weeks from
today, which shall be unconditional bank guarantee as agreed by the learned
senior counsel appearing for the petitioner and same shall be kept alive during
the pendency of the arbitration proceedings.
5. It would be open to the respondent herein to seek for appropriate
orders from the Arbitral Tribunal for release of the said bank guarantee or
invoking the same and realising the proceeds thereof. In the event of said
request being made it is open to the Arbitral Tribunal to consider the same on
its own merits and we make it explicitly clear that we have not expressed any
opinion in that regard. However, it is also pertinent to note at this juncture,
itself that the petitioner herein while responding to the notice issued by the
respondent in the reply notice issued on 21.09.2024 has acknowledged its
liability to an extent of Rs. 6,69,52,278/-(Rs. Six Crore Sixty Nine Lakh Fifty Two
Thousand Two Hundred Seventy Eight only). This fact can be taken note of by
the Arbitral Tribunal while considering the prayer, if any, made for release of the
amount covered under the bank guarantee by the respondent herein.
6. It is needless to state, that petition which has been filed under
Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 would not survive for
consideration which is also agreed upon by the learned counsels appearing for
the parties and as such the jurisdictional Commercial Court can consign the said
proceedings to records.
7. Both parties are at liberty to work out their rights in the pending
arbitral proceedings in accordance with law, as observed hereinabove.
8. The contempt proceedings initiated by the respondent against the
petitioner for non-compliance of the direction issued by the Commercial Court
3

## Page 546

on 10.02.2026 would also not survive for consideration and the same shall also
be consigned to records.
9. In view of the above, the present petition stands disposed of.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stands disposed of.

THE SCHEDULED TRIBE CERTIFICATE 
SCRUTINY COMMITTEE    Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. Leave granted. 
3. Despite due service of notice, no one has entered  
appearance on behalf of the sole respondent. 
4. Heard learned counsel for the appellant.
5. These appeal are against the orders dated 13.01.2026 and
16.03.2026 passed by the High Court of judicature at Bombay in
Civil Application (W) No. 60 of 2026 in Writ Petition No. 3940
of 2023 and in Misc. Civil Application No. 180 of 2026 in Writ
Petition No. 3940 of 2023 respectively.
6. In the first order, the appellant sought to withdraw the
Writ Petition against an order dated 11.05.2023 passed by the
respondent-Committee  and  the  High  Court  while  granting
permission to withdraw the Writ Petition refused to grant
liberty  for  filing  a  fresh  petition.  Subsequently,  the
appellant approached the High Court for review of the first
1

## Page 565

order by stating that she did not intend to withdraw the Writ
Petition. By the second order impugned before us, the High
Court refused to entertain the Miscellaneous Civil Application
for review. 
7. Having considered the matter, we are of the opinion that
the  High  Court  should  have  granted  the  permission  for
restitution  of  the  Writ  Petition  for  the  circumstances
explained in the Miscellaneous Civil Application for review. A
Writ Petition under Article 226 is in exercise of a precious
constitutional remedy and the High Court could have been a
little more liberal in entertaining the application. This has
got nothing to do with the merits of the matter and even we
are not expressing any opinion on the merits of the case. 
8. In view of the above, we set aside the orders dated
13.01.2026 and 16.03.2026 passed by the High Court and allow
the appeals. The Writ Petition is restored to its original
number. The High Court may proceed to consider the Writ
Petition on its own merits. 
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO……………..OF 2026
(@Special Leave Petition (Civil) No.5179 of 2020)
THE ALARANATH DHANDA MULAKA 
MAHAVIDYALAYA THROUGH 
SECRETARY CUM PRINCIPAL                                         … APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
LAXMIDHARA SAMANTASINGHARA (DEAD)
THR. LRS. & ORS.                                                             …RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. On 4 th of October 1978, a gift deed of an immovable property was
executed in favour of the present appellant – original Defendant No.1, by
Defendant No.2 – the father of the plaintiffs.
3. On the said land, Defendant No.1 set up a college which has been
functional since September 1981.  Sometime in the year 1989, the plaintiffs,
sons of Defendant No.2, filed a suit seeking a declaration qua the said gift deed
to be illegal and void on the premise that the suit land was not the individual
property of Defendant No.2, but joint family property in which the plaintiffs
also had an interest.  The suit was decreed  ex  parte  vide  judgment dated
01.07.2000.  Significantly, the plaintiffs sat over the decree till the year 2016
1

## Page 571

i.e., 15 years and thereafter only filed an application for execution.  It is at this
point in time, the donee i.e., Defendant No.1 learnt about the decree ex parte in
nature, to have been passed with respect to the suit land.  Resultantly, Defendant
No.1 took steps in accordance with law. 
 
4. The District and Sessions Judge vide judgment dated 08.02.2018 in RFA
No.31 of 2016 set aside the said ex parte decree by condoning the delay of 15
years and 7 months.  However, the High Court vide order dated 18.09.2019 in
CRP No.4 of 2018 set aside the same, for the Defendant No.1 did not furnish
sufficient explanation on the issue of delay.  It is in the aforesaid backdrop we
are called upon to decide the present appeal.
5.      It is a matter of record that certain facts are undisputed.  The suit property
was gifted in the year 1978 by Defendant No.2 in favour of Defendant No.1.
Soon thereafter, i.e., from 21.09.1981, an educational institution was set up
which became functional.  It was only in the year 1989 that a suit was filed,
challenging the said gift deed, in which Defendant No.1 was proceeded  ex
parte.     Defendant No.1 is in possession the possession of the property.
Defendant  No.2  even  though  associated  with  Defendant  No.1,  never  ever
informed him/Defendant No.1 of the passing of decree.  The execution of the
decree was put on hold for over 15 years. 
 
6.     Having heard learned counsel for the parties, we are of the considered view
that the High Court committed a grave error in entertaining the revision petition
and setting aside the order dated 08.02.2018 passed by the District Judge, Puri,
who  allowed  the  application  under  Section  5  of  the  Limitation  Act  by
entertaining the regular first appeal.  It is argued that the decree which is
collusive in nature, was only obtained to defeat the right of a party, more so on
account of the prices of the land having risen considerably.  While we refrain
2

## Page 572

from commenting about the conduct of either the plaintiff or their father i.e.,
Defendant No.2, but considering the overall conspectus, we are inclined to
interfere with the impugned order, for Defendant No.2  did furnish sufficient
explanation in taking recourse to such steps as were permissible in law, in
getting an ex parte decree set aside.  
7. It is argued that the suit was not maintainable in view of the applicable
municipal law(s).  We are not making any observation on the same and leave the
issue open for the same to be considered during trial.  The appeal is allowed.
The  ex parte  decree dated 01.07.2000 in T.S.No.159/1989  titled  Sri Kapila
Samantisinghar & ors.  vs. The Alarnath Dhanda Mulaka Mahavidyalaya,
Managing Committee represented through its Secretary and Anr. , is quashed
and set aside.  The suit is restored to its original number for it to be tried on
expeditious basis in accordance with law.  Parties to appeal before the Trial
Court on 08.09.2026.  Pending applications(s) if any shall stand disposed of.

I.A. No. 186836/2026 has been filed by Mr. Vaibhav
Dubey as the new Advocate on Record for the petitioner in
place of the erstwhile Counsel. He submits that it was
necessitated as the petitioner was not in a position to
1

## Page 574

SLP (C) NO.15498/2016
pay as per the directions of this Court in its order
dated 13.04.2026 and thus, modification/recall of the
said order is sought.
2. We may pause here to indicate that on 13.04.2026, the
Court had passed the following order:
“Heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. It  is  not  in  dispute  that  order  dated
29.04.2022 passed by this Court in the present
proceedings directing the petitioner by way of
an  interim  arrangement  to  pay  Rs.20,000/-
(Rupees  Twenty  Thousand)  per  month  to  the
respondent-wife  for  maintenance  of  their
daughter, has not been complied with despite
repeated opportunities being granted.
3. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits
that he has filed an affidavit bringing on
record  the  details  of  his  assets,  which
discloses that he is not in a position to pay
the maintenance amount.
4. Be that as it may, the order having attained
finality due to efflux of time and till date no
petition/application having been filed praying
for recall/modification of the said order, the
Court finds that the order has to be complied
with.
5. Accordingly, we direct the learned Family
Court, Bengaluru, to ensure payment of the
amount in terms of the order dated 29.04.2022
passed  by  this  Court  in  the  present
proceedings, by taking all necessary measures
including  coercive  steps,  against  the
petitioner herein, in accordance with law.  The
Court shall submit a report of compliance.
6. Registry shall communicate this order to the
concerned Family Court forthwith.
7. List on 29.07.2026.
8. Further, the i nterim order passed by this
2

## Page 575

Court on 05.07.2016 stands withdrawn.”
3. On a query of the Court to Mr. Vaibhav Dubey, learned
counsel, as to whether the said order has been complied
with. He fairly submits that the same has not been
complied with as the petitioner is not in a capacity to
pay the same.
4. Having considered the matter, we find no ground to
modify or recall our order dated 13.04.2026. Accordingly,
I.A. No.186836/2026 stands dismissed.
5. At this juncture, Mrs. Vaijayanthi Girish, erstwhile
learned Advocate on Record appearing for the petitioner
stands discharged from the present matter, as Mr. Vaibhav
Dubey,  learned  counsel  has  already  filed  a  fresh
vakalatnama. 
6. Having considered the matter in its entirety and
going through the material available on record and also
taking into account what has been recorded in the earlier
order dated 13.04.2026, we do not find any ground made
out for interference in the present matter.
7.  Accordingly,  the  Special  Leave  Petition  stands
dismissed.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

1. This petition seeks Special Leave to Appeal against
the impugned judgment and order dated 20.03.2026 passed
by the Division Bench of the High Court of Judicature of
Jharkhand at Ranchi in IA. No.16603 of 2025 in Cr. Appeal
(DB) No. 566/2024, whereby the High Court rejected the
petitioner’s  application  for  suspension  of  sentence
during the pendency of his appeal.
2. By judgment dated 20.03.2024 passed by the Special
Judge  under  N.D.P.S.Act,  Palamau  at  Daltongan  the
Petitioner  was  convicted  under  Section  15(C)  of  the
Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (for
short “the NDPS Act”) for possessing 700 Kgs of poppy
straw and sentenced him to twenty years of rigorous
imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 2,00,000/- and additional six
months of rigorous imprisonment in case of default.
3. Having heard learned counsel for both parties and
having perused the material on record, without expressing
any final opinion on the merits of the appeal, we are of
the  considered  view  that  a  prima  facie  case  for
suspension  of  sentence  is  made  out,  given  that  the
petitioner has undergone more than three years in custody
SLP(Crl.) No.14930/2026                                         2

## Page 635

and  the  arguable  legal  issues  raised  regarding  the
sampling  of  the  contraband  during  the  process  of
investigation.
4. Accordingly,  the  execution  of  the  substantive
sentence of imprisonment awarded to the petitioner in FIR
No.40/2023, P.S. Palamau, Sadar, Jharkhand, shall remain
suspended during the pendency of the appeal before the
High Court.  
5. The Special Judge under N.D.P.S. Act, Palamau at
Daltongan  shall release the petitioner on bail on such
conditions as deemed fit and appropriate, on the basis of
the suspension of sentence granted by us. In the event of
breach of any conditions specified above, it shall be
open to the State to move an application before the
jurisdictional Sessions Court for cancellation of bail.
6. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of in the
above terms.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

VIKAS JINDAL                            PETITIONER(S)
                                VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA & ORS.                   RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R 
1. Even on the second call, there is no appearance
on behalf of the petitioner.
2. The  petitioner  has  filed  the  present  writ
petition before this Court, seeking a declaration
that Sections 69 and 70(1) of the Central Goods and
Services Tax Act, 2017, are unconstitutional.
3. Mr.  S.  Dwarakanath,  learned  Additional
Solicitor General appearing for the respondents, at
the outset, has drawn the attention of this Court to
the judgment delivered in Radhika Agarwal v. Union
of India and Others, (2025) 6 SCC 545. In  paragraph
79  of  the  aforesaid  judgment,  this  Court  has
rejected the challenge to the vires of Sections 69
and 70 of the CGST Act. Paragraph 79 reads as under:
“79. Thus, a penalty or prosecution mechanism
for the levy and collection of GST, and for
checking  its  evasion,  is  a  permissible
exercise of legislative power. The GST Acts,
in pith and substance, pertain to Article 246-
A  of  the  Constitution  and  the  powers  to
summon, arrest and prosecute are ancillary and
WRIT PETITION (CRIMINAL)  NO.33/2025

## Page 655

2
incidental to the power to levy and collect
goods  and  services  tax.  In  view  of  the
aforesaid, the vires challenge to Section 69
and 70 of the CGST Act must fail and is
accordingly rejected.” 
4. In light of the aforesaid judgment, no further
orders are required in the present writ petition. The
same is accordingly dismissed. 
5.  Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed
of.

## Page 673

3. Since no orders adverse to the interest of the respondent is being passed,
notice to respondent is not issued.
4. The respondent was enrolled in the Indian Army on 12.03.2004, came to be
discharged on 16.02.2026 and challenge laid to the same by filing Writ Petition
No.1933/2007, did not yield any result, or in other words, the Writ Petition came
to be dismissed by order dated 21.05.2008. Hence, respondent filed an intra-
court appeal in DB SAW No.1273/2011, which came to be allowed after 18 years
on 25.09.2024. A review application in WRW No.120/2025 has been filed
seeking review of the order 25.09.2024 in several grounds urged therein, in the
interregnum, the respondent herein who was successful before the Division
Bench, initiated contempt proceedings in Contempt Petition No.811/2025 and
this having been brought to the notice of the learned Division Bench hearing the
Contempt Petition, persuaded the said Division Bench to list Review Petition
along with Contempt Petition vide order dated 25.05.2026 and adjourned the
matter to 06.07.2026.
5.  Surprisingly on the said dated i.e. 06.07.2026, the Division Bench seems to
have directed the respondent(s) to appear before the Court and show cause as
to why they should not be punished for willfully disobeying the order dated
25.09.2024, which was the subject matter of the Review Petition No.120/2025,
which undisputedly was ordered to be tagged along with the Contempt Petition.
If it were to be so, the course open to the Division Bench was to hear both the
matters or hear the Review Petition at the outset and thereafter pass
appropriate orders on Contempt Petition, if required, in the Contempt Petition.
Surprisingly, the Division Bench seems to have been pursuaded to accept the
Contempt Petition alone notwithstanding that the Review Petition was pending
which had already been ordered to be tagged with the Contempt Petition.
2

## Page 674

6. As such, in the facts obtained in the instant case, it would not appropriate to
de-link the Review Petition from the Contempt Petition and as such we request
the High Court to take up the Review Petition and dispose of the same on merits
and in accordance with law without being influenced by its order dated
06.07.2026 passed in the Contempt proceedings and till the Review Petition is
disposed of, the Contempt proceedings shall remain stayed.
7.  It is made clear that on disposal of the Review Petition, the Court
adjudicating the Contempt Petition, would be at liberty to proceed on its own
merits without being influenced by its earlier observations. Accordingly, the
Special Leave Petition stands disposed of.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
(RASHI GUPTA)                                   (AVGV RAMU)
COURT MASTER (SH)                             COURT MASTER (NSH)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.          /2026
(@ SLP (CRL.) No. 1335/2026)
SUKHJINDER KAUR  APPELLANT(S)
          VERSUS
STATE OF PUNJAB & ORS.    RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. The appellant, Sukhjinder Kaur, is the mother of the deceased
and was the complainant in First Information Report(FIR) No.
263/2020 dated 16.07.2020 registered with Police Station –
Civil  Lines  Batala,  District  –  Batala,  Punjab,  for  the
offences punishable under Sections 306 and 34 of the Code of
Criminal Procedure, 1973. 
3. By the impugned judgment/order dated 31.10.2025, a learned
Judge of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana, Chandigarh,
quashed the aforestated FIR and the further proceedings based
thereon, without taking into consideration a crucial piece of
evidence upon which the prosecution placed reliance. This was
a video stated to have been recorded by the deceased prior to
committing suicide, wherein he is stated to have implicated
the accused in that context. Without taking note of this
1

## Page 685

video, as is evident from the fact that no reference has been
made thereto in the body of the impugned judgment/order, the
learned Judge deemed it fit to allow the petition filed by the
accused and quashed the FIR and all consequential proce edings
arising therefrom. 
4. This approach on the part of the High Court in eschewing from
consideration  a  relevant  piece  of  evidence  cannot  be
countenanced. 
5. In such circumstances, we are of the opinion that it would be
appropriate that the High Court reconsiders the matter taking
all aspects into consideration. 
6. The  appeal  is,  accordingly,  allowed,  setting  aside  the
impugned judgment/order. C.R.M.-M No. 8786/2023 shall stand
restored to the file of the High Court for consideration
afresh on merits and in accordance with law. 
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

                             O R D E R
At the outset, learned counsels for the parties submit that
the mediation is in progress and is likely to take some more time.
2. At this juncture, learned counsel for the petitioners submits
that despite a specific order passed by this Court on 13.04.2026
that the parties would be required to appear physically before the
learned Mediator, if the learned Mediator so desires, on the last
occasion i.e., on 28.07.2026, the parties were asked to appear
physically before the learned Mediator. However, the petitioner
no.1-wife was present physically before the learned Mediator but
the respondent no.1-husband did not turn up. It was further
submitted that in the said order dated 13.04.2026, this Court had
also directed that whenever the petitioner no.1-wife was required
to be physically present before the learned Mediator, she would be
entitled to reimbursement quantified at Rs.5,000/- (Rupees Five
Thousand) per visit. It was submitted that the same has also not
been paid. It was submitted that even the direction to continue
paying Rs.6,500/- (Rupees Six Thousand Five Hundred) per month as
maintenance, has also not been complied with by the respondent
no.1-husband.
3. Learned counsel for the respondent no.1 is not readily in a
position to rebut or take a stand on such submissions.
4. If the aforesaid is true, the Court would take serious note of
the same. However, before passing any order, it is made clear that
within two days from today, the up-to-date arrears of maintenance

## Page 704

3
be cleared and Rs.5,000/- (Rupees Five Thousand), as directed, be
also transferred into the bank account of the petitioner no.1-wife
by the respondent no.1-husband, failing which on the next date of
listing, the Court may not show any leniency.
5. Further, it is indicated that if the respondent no.1-husband
fails  to  cooperate  in  the  mediation  proceedings  as  per  the
direction of the learned Mediator, it will be a ground for this
Court to pass stringent order against the respondent no.1-husband.
6. List on 30.09.2026.

## Page 745

2
2. Exemption Application is allowed.
3. This petition arises from the Order passed by the High Court
of Jharkhand dated 18th September, 2025 in Criminal Miscellaneous
Petition No. 1737 of 2022, by which the petition preferred by the
petitioner  seeking  quashing  of  the  criminal  proceedings  in
connection with RC Case No. 07(A)/2016-R pending in the Court of
Additional Judicial Commissioner-XVI-cum-Special Judge, CBI, Ranchi
came to be dismissed. To put it in other words, the High Court
declined to quash the criminal proceedings against the petitioner
before us.
4. We take notice of the fact that along with the present
petitioner, there are other co-accused, and being public servants,
are charged with the offence of criminal conspiracy punishable
under Section 120B of the IPC, and Section 13(2) read with 13(1)(d)
of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (for short, "the Act,
1988") respectively.
5. The petitioner came before us at a point of time when charge
was already framed by the Special Judge.
6. Today, we are informed that the Trial Court has started
recording the oral evidence.
7. Mr. Lekni, the learned Senior Counsel has manifold contentions
to raise before us, more particularly, according to him, no case
worth the name is made out insofar as the involvement of his
client, as alleged, is concerned.
8. We do not propose to express any opinion, even prima facie, at
this stage, since the trial has already commenced. Let the evidence
come on record, and based on it, the Trial Court shall decide
whether the prosecution has been able to establish the charge or
not. 
9. It shall be open for the petitioner to raise all contentions
available  to  him  in  law  before  the  Trial  Court.
10. The Trial Court shall decide the guilt or the innocence of the
petitioner strictly on the basis of the evidence that may come on
record, without being influenced in any manner by any of the
observations  made  by  the  High  Court  in  its  impugned  order.

right of a protected tenant has not been determined by the

(Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950,
the protected tenant holds the land, whether physically in
possession or not.
2. It is further contended that the Joint Collector,
vide its order dated 31.10.1979, remanded the matter to the
Revenue Divisional Officer (RDO) for fresh inquiry, after
notice to all the parties, principally on the ground that
no notice had been served on the protected tenants, i.e.
the petitioners. However, this order has been challenged
and now set aside by the High Court.
3. We are alive to the position that the SLP (C)
No.14163/2026 against the same impugned order has not been
entertained by us, however, after hearing learned Senior
Counsel appearing for the petitioner at length, we feel
that the matter requires consideration in view of  Thota
Sridhar Reddy (supra).

four weeks.

O R D E R
1. There is an enormous delay of 489 days in filing the Review
Petition(s).  The  application  for  condonation  of  delay  in
filing the Review Petition(s) does not give sufficient cause. 
2. Even otherwise, having perused the Review Petition, we find
that there is no error apparent on the face of the record. No
case for review under Order XLVII Rule 1 of the Supreme Court
Rules 2013 has been established.
3.   In view of the above, the Review Petition is dismissed on
the ground of delay as well as on merits.

the fact that the minor child has distanced itself from the father
for long number of years, namely, eight years, a platform or a
conducive atmosphere for interacting with the father would be
required to be created. In other words, the expertise of a Child
Counsellor would be warranted. In these circumstances, we direct
1

## Page 1022

the Member Secretary, DLSA, Jaipur to identify a Child Counsellor
and intimate respondent No.1 – mother to take the child to such
Counsellor on such date that may be convenient to the Child
Counsellor and the parties. The father, mother and child shall
appear before the said Child Counsellor, who shall interact with
the child and make efforts to create a conducive atmosphere for the
father to have interaction with the child in the presence of the
Counsellor. In the event of such interaction not being possible at
the first instance, the Child Counsellor would be at liberty to fix
such further date or dates as he/she may deem fit and appropriate
and as an expert, he/she would be in a better position to take the
call in that regard. Such counselling session shall be held at such
place the Child Consellor may decide keeping in mind the paramount
interest of child. 
3. The  outcome  of  such  interaction  /  interactions  may  be
submitted to this Court by way of a report in a sealed envelope
through Member Secretary, DLSA, Jaipur and the tentative charges,
if any, shall also be intimated to this Court to enable the
petitioner – father to pay the said amount to the Child Counsellor.
4. List after report is received from Member Secretary, DLSA,
Jaipur.

   UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1.  The present petitions have been filed against the impugned order dated
11.08.2026 whereby the High Court had issued notice, however, declined to
grant stay in the matter.

## Page 1234

2. Learned counsel for the petitioner has pointed out from the impugned order
that now the matter is kept on 17.12.2026 and therefore the stay, as prayed
for, may be granted in favour of the present petitioner.
3. However, we are of the view that when the matter is pending before the High
Court, we are not inclined to interfere with the aforesaid order. However, we
grant liberty to the petitioner to file an application for preponement of the
matter. As and when such application is filed, the High Court shall consider such
application made by the petitioner for preponement of the matter in accordance
with law.
4. At this stage, it has also been pointed out by the learned counsel for the
petitioner that after the High Court had issued notice on 11.08.2026, on the
very  next  date  i.e.  on  12.08.2026,  the  Investigating  Officer  has  filed  the
chargesheet. Hence, liberty is reserved to the petitioner to file an amendment
application before the High Court. As and when such application for amendment
is filed, it is open for the High Court to examine the same in accordance with
law.
5.  With the aforesaid observations, the Special Leave Petitions stand disposed
of.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

to 6.
2. Delay condoned.
3. Respondent No(s).4 to 6 have filed O.S. No.535 of  
2024 for declaration of title and possession, amongst  
others. The same is pending at the injunction stage. In 
the  meanwhile,  on  the  revenue  side,  the  Deputy  
Commissioner passed an order on 13.09.2024, declaring  
mutation  entry  in  the  name  of  the  aforesaid  
respondent(s) over the suit land.
4. We make it clear that since the civil suit is  
pending, the findings of the revenue authorities as  
well as that of the High Court insofar mutation entry  
is concerned, would abide by the finding in the civil  
suit and any observations made by the High Court would  
not come in the way of determination of the inter-party 
rights in the suit. Needless to say, the observations  
made by the Deputy Commissioner regarding possession of 
the suit property would not be determinative and also  
not binding on the parties.
5. With the above observation(s), the Special Leave  
Petition is disposed of.
6. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand  
disposed of.

I.A. No. 156384/2026
1. The applicant/petitioner seeks extension of time to surrender.
2. Concededly,  the  I.A.  No.  101147/2026  moved  by  the
applicant/petitioner seeking exemption to surrender was rejected by
this Court on 10.04.2026, however she was granted four weeks’ time
to surrender and furnish the surrender certificate.
3. But rather than complying with the order, referred to above,
the present application has been moved for extension of time. 

## Page 1348

2
4. In brief, all what is stated is that post order dated
10.04.2026, the applicant/petitioner met with an accident and is
thus under medical treatment. Therefore, the time granted to the
applicant/petitioner to surrender may be extended till she is fully
fit.
5. Ex  facie  the time granted to the applicant/petitioner  vide
order  dated  10.04.2026  lapsed  on  09.05.2026.  The  present
application has been moved four months after the said order.
Although the averments set out in the application do not inspire
much confidence but in the totality of facts and circumstances, the
applicant/petitioner  is  granted  two  weeks’  further  time  to
surrender. Accordingly, learned counsel for the applicant shall
ensure that a surrender certificate is furnished with the office.
It is made clear that in the event of default, appropriate order
shall follow.
6. The application is disposed of in the above terms.

1. Delay condoned.
2. This application has been filed for correction of a factual
error pointed out in our order dated 03.04.2025. It is stated by
the learned counsel for the applicant-petitioner (wife) that no
child was born from the wedlock and a factually incorrect averment
was inadvertently made in the Transfer Petition, due to which
paragraph No. 1 of the order dated 03.04.2025 has recorded a wrong
fact.
1

## Page 1404

3. Further, an affidavit has been filed in support of the
application, stating that no child was ever born from the wedlock.
4. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
5. In view of the categorical averment made in the affidavit that
an inadvertent mistake was committed by the advocate of the
applicant while drafting the transfer petition, we accept the
prayer in this application and order the necessary correction in
our order dated 03.04.2025.  Paragraph 1 of the said order shall
now read as follows:
“The petitioner and the respondent no.1 got married on
12.12.2019.  There arose some matrimonial dispute, as a
result of which, cross-cases have been filed by the
parties. Respondent no.1 – husband filed a Divorce
Petition No.FSUIT No.29/2001 at Surat which has already
been transferred by this Court to Auriya, Uttar Pradesh
vide an order dated 20.01.2023.”
6. Ordered accordingly.
7. The Registry is directed to issue a corrected certified copy
of the order dated 03.04.2025.
8. As regards the plea sought to be raised by the respondent-
husband, suffice it to say that he shall be at liberty to take such
plea and prove the same before the concerned court in accordance
with law.
9.  IA  No.  147051/2026  and  Miscellaneous  Application  stand
disposed of, accordingly.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We have heard Dr. Abhishek Manu Singhvi and Mr. Ranjit Kumar,
learned senior counsel appearing on behalf of the Petitioners.
2. Having regard to the fact that the High Court in Dammalapati
Srinivas v. State of Andhra Pradesh, 2021 SCC OnLine AP 2706  had
quashed the criminal proceedings under Section 13(1)(d)(ii) of the
Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 pertaining to the same land
pooling scheme of the Government of Andhra Pradesh, and that
judgment was upheld by this Court in State of Andhra Pradesh v.
Chekka Guru Murali Mohan & Ors., (2022) 20 SCC 574 , it seems to us
that quashing of the proceedings is a natural consequence and,
thus, calls for no interference by this Court. However, it is
clarified that the impugned judgment and our order are based on the
facts and circumstances of the case in hand and shall have no
bearing on the other cases, which shall be dealt with by the High
Court on their own merits.
3. The Special Leave Petitions stand disposed of, with pending
application(s), if any.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The instant Writ Petition purportedly filed in public interest
seeks directions for framing appropriate guidelines on the use of
Artificial Intelligence (AI) and other tools by the Government and
its  instrumentalities  for  the  purposes  of  welfare  scheme
governance, surveillance, policing and online content moderation.  
2. The petitioner, who is a practicing advocate in the Supreme
Court, asserts that unregulated and non-transparent deployment of
AI and other such technologies like Machine Learning by the State
and its instrumentalities in matters of deciding welfare scheme
entitlements, policing and social media content regulation has a
direct impact on civil liberties, privacy, dignity and livelihood
of people.  As regards the issues pertaining to the formulation of
appropriate policies and/or regulations for governing the use of AI
1

## Page 1530

or  similar  tools,  the  petitioner  has  already  submitted  a
comprehensive representation on 10.02.2026, a copy whereof has been
placed on record as Annexure P/5.   We find that, in addition to
the aforesaid representation, the Writ Petition also contains
comprehensive averments regarding the issues outlined above.  
3. We, therefore, dispose of the Writ Petition at this stage,
without expressing any opinion on the merits, and direct the
respondents to duly consider the petitioner’s suggestions for the
purposes of taking appropriate measures.  The petitioner shall be
at liberty to supplement his representation by forwarding a copy of
the Writ Petition to the respondents.
4. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand closed.

                             O R D E R
We   fail  to understand  as  to  how  the
petitioner/Department  once  having  “noted”  that  order  dated
22.01.2024  was  assailed  before  this  Court  in  SLP  (C)
D.No.41292/2025 (T he Principal Commissioner of Income Tax  1 ,
Vadodara Vs. M /s Gujarat Narmada Valley Fertilizers and Chemicals

## Page 1542

- 2 -
the ground of 463 days delay, subsequently, in February, 2026, this
special leave petition has been filed with 739 days delay against
the very same impugned order.  This is an instance of unnecessarily
burdening this Court with a frivolous special leave petition. 
We hope that the Department would take note of the aforesaid
observations and be more vigilant in filing cases with exorbitant
delay before this Court and repeatedly not file such cases. 
With the aforesaid observations, the Special Leave Petition is
dismissed on the ground of delay leaving open the question of law,
if any.
Pending  application(s)  shall stand disposed of.
